en: Ruyyaka [Rājānaka]:
*Vyaktivivekavyākhyā*, Second Vimarśa; now begins the second chapter.

Thus, having first refuted the definition of *dhvani* in the initial inquiry, he says "In this regard, indeed," and so forth, in order to refute another section of the *Dhvani-śāstra* by generally establishing an elaborate array of defects consisting of the manifestation of impropriety (*anaucitya*) within poetry.
Thus it has been stated by the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
It is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it is directly the object of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
By "the former ones" (*ādyaiḥ*) is meant Dhvanikāra and others. As it has been said:
Nothing causes the disruption of rasa except impropriety;
indeed, the composition of well-known propriety is the supreme secret of rasa.

By such statements as these, since the conclusion ultimately rests upon the *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) by way of what is expressed (*vācya*), there occurs: (1) *avimarśa*, which is the failure to attend to—that is, the neglect of—the primary object intended to be conveyed;

(2) *prakramabheda*, which is the deviation from the commencement—that is, the alteration midway or the improper completion—of the undertaking of some matter due to its being subordinated [to another];
and (3) *vyutkrama*, which is the breaking of the sequence—that is, the transgression of the established order.
Tautology (*paunaruktya*) is restatement;
non-statement (*avacana*) is the failure to express what ought to be said.
These five types of fallacies (*dūṣaṇajāti*) are distinguished by their internal subdivisions.
Regarding this pentad of defects, such as the failure to deliberate upon what ought to be done, which has been raised here by the author of the work by resorting to the path of inquiry—
one should not show disregard out of envy toward the intellect of a person of the present day alone;
for such an inquiry, consisting in the pointing out of these very defects, was already set forth by the ancients themselves.

For instance, by demonstrating the non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case in expressions such as *dāsyāḥ putraḥ* ("the son of a slave-girl") when used in an abusive sense, the author of the Sūtras has clearly indicated a lack of consideration for what is actually to be prescribed (*vidheya*).

Likewise, in the sūtra *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyāda-* (Pāṇini 2.3.39), the author of the Bhāṣya— by stating that [the construction] does not occur in cases such as *gavāṃ svāmī* ("owner of cows") and *aśveṣu* ("in horses")— has explicitly demonstrated a break in the logical consistency of the initial approach (*prakramabheda*).

Likewise, regarding the rule that *kṛñ* is employed after [a verb] in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense—as in *iy ānañja*—the mention of the word "after" (*anu*) implies that the subsequent employment [of *kṛñ*] precludes its placement immediately before [the verbal root], as seen in examples such as *taṃ pātayām prathamam āsa*. Furthermore, by explaining the restriction on usage through the rule that particles (*ca*-class words) do not occur [independently], as in *na hi bhavati ca vṛkṣaḥ*, the author indicates their status as mere indicators (*dyotaka*). Thus, he has indeed implicitly pointed out the violation of the proper sequence, characterized by the employment [of a particle] in an improper place.

Likewise, Kātyāyana—who, considering the economy of grammatical operation (*vṛttilāghava*), held that a *bahuvrīhi* compound should take precedence over a *karmadhāraya* or a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) due to its brevity—has indeed already revealed the redundancy [of the rule]. Similarly, in the context of the rule *īṣadasamāptau*, he refutes the definition of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) stated by the author of the Sūtras—which is to be understood through the very declaration [itself]—by asserting instead that the suffixes *kalpa* and so forth are prescribed for things similar to the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). Thus, he treats as the actual subject matter of the declaration that which is to be understood from the declaration itself.
By establishing a simile, even the non-statement of what is to be expressed (vācyāvacana) is indeed illuminated by means of the basis of the simile;
likewise, by means of the basis of a metaphor (rūpaka), even the statement of what is not to be expressed (avācyavacana) is indeed illuminated.

Thus, following the path of the great scholars and reflecting with a respectful regard for the instruction of those possessed of aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya), there is no occasion for even a trace of censure against this man of great intelligence; so, enough of this prolixity.
"And of this" refers generally to impropriety (*anaucitya*).

They are called "defects" (*doṣa*) because they corrupt the poem by bringing about its deformity. Regarding the term "simpleton" (*mugdha*), there are three causes for one who is questioned not responding with a distorted [or improper] reply.

In this context, these [faults] are stated in sequence because they are subject to doubt: *maugdhyam* (childishness), characterized by an inability to provide a reply; *asahyatvam* (intolerance), which is a state of immaturity even when one possesses *pratibhāna* (insight); and *mātsaryam* (envy), characterized by an inability to endure the virtues of others even when one is mature.
In the phrase "yaḥ kila," there is a pause (*cheda*) right here.

By the words "at the request of the student" (*chātrābhyarthanayā*), there is an indication of both the acceptance of the role of questioner (*praṣṭṛtva*) and the role of respondent (*prativaktṛtva*).
*Paurobhāgya* means the state of being exclusively focused on finding faults.

Now, if an examination of faults is conducted in another's poetry for the sake of their avoidance, why then is there no such avoidance of them in one's own poetry? And if it is asked, "Does he not perhaps resort to the silence of envy?"—in response to this, the word *iti* should be indicated in the sequence immediately following [the question]. Since it is indicated in a different order, a deviation from the proper sequence is not appropriate.
In this same way, other [examples] such as the *śokāpadāna* (the account of sorrow) should be understood.

To that end, he says: "in his own compositions" (*svakṛtiṣu*). "Composition" (*kṛti*) means poetry (*kāvyam*). Regarding the term "fury" (*saṃrambha*): "elephant-insects" (*karikīṭāḥ*) refers to contemptible elephants; it is a compound formed according to the rule "contemptible things [are expressed] by means of contemptuous terms."
The comparison of ants to elephants is made with respect to their hopes;

likewise, fragments of clouds are compared to the clouds at the end of an eon—this is the division of the verse. This stanza has been explained in detail in the *Vakroktijīvita*, so it should be understood from that very source.
The word "tāvat" indicates the introduction of the three-fold lack of discernment regarding the predicate (*vidheya*) contained within this verse.

Regarding the phrase "because of the possibility of a connection," the underlying intention is as follows: according to the rule "a grammatical operation concerning words [is applied] when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), a compound (*samāsa*) is caused by semantic connection (*sāmarthya*).
And semantic competency (sāmarthya) consists in the state of having a coherent meaning;
coherence, in turn, is a relationship. And in this context, that relationship is the qualifier-qualified relation (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva).
Just as in the case of "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a qualifier of a relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*),
and since a relative exclusion is not possible here according to the logic that will be stated later—
[one might ask: "But how can the negative particle in 'non-Brahmin' and similar cases be a qualifier?"
For a qualifier serves to color the qualified;
however, the word "not" (nañ), due to its contradictory nature, does not color an affirmation. Therefore, how can it function as a qualifier?
This is not so;
in expressions such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), the word "Brahmin" refers to those similar to a Brahmin, such as Kṣatriyas and others.
And this application of the word "Brahmin" to non-Kṣatriyas and the like is indicated by the negative particle *nañ*.

Thus it has been said: "When joined with *nañ* or *iva*, [a word] refers to something other than that, or to its similar; for such is the meaning. And in this regard, the cause is the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*).
How this is so should be understood from the Bhāṣya on the *nañ*-sūtra.
Regarding the term "predominance":

where there is predominance of the injunction (*vidhi*) and non-predominance of the negation (*pratiṣedha*), where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the subsequent word, where there is a determinative compound (*samartha-samāsa*), and where there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), there is exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
This is because of the conclusion [in the *Paddhati*]: "Exclusion is the instruction of something by setting aside something else."
In this regard, three things are explicitly taught in the verse, while two are implied by the word *jugopa*.

Here, there is a positive injunction regarding the meaning of the latter member of the compound as qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), rather than a prohibition of qualities such as being terrified.

In that case as well, since [the state of] being unafraid and so forth is already established, the acts of concealment and so on are enjoined by way of restating that [established fact]; thus, there is the status of a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation).
Regarding "non-primacy":

where the negation is primary and the injunction is non-primary, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verbal action, resulting in either an *asamartha-samāsa* (compound of incompatible meanings) or a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
In this context, *prasajyapratiṣedha* is a negation that follows after having first applied [the predicate].
In this verse, when the triad is specified, the other two are implied by the phrase "or not" (*na vā*).
In this case, a prohibition directed toward a haughty night-stalker is understood,
rather than an injunction for a non-haughty night-stalker; thus,
it is a prasajya-pratiṣedha (absolute negation), for here there is a prohibition of one who possesses fury.
The meaning is that there is a negation—according to the logic to be explained later—of that person who is agitated, of the agitation residing in him, and of the act of agitating.
"The injunction for one not agitated" means the injunction for one who is similar to one not agitated, namely, one who performs an action similar to agitation but is essentially indifferent.
This refers to what was stated: "as if joined with the negative particle," and so forth.
In that context, "therein" refers to the negation of one who is like an enraged person.
"And not this" he negates;
"the position of its establishment" means the position of establishing the intended object, which is characterized by the primary negation.

Regarding this state of being an injunction and a restatement: "of this" refers to the fact that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the injunction, while the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound is the restatement.
For in a compound, the meaning of the subsequent member, having the meaning of the negative particle as its subordinate element, is perceived as the primary sense.
Regarding the phrase "kāvyārtha" (the meaning of poetry):
here, having first demonstrated the *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) as that which is to be excluded, he illustrates the *paryudāsa* (relative negation) as that which is to be determined.

Now, one might object: if the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with a verb in an absolute negation, then in the expression "asaṃrabdhahavān," there would be a negation of the action of agitation (*saṃrambha*).
To the question, "What fault is there in this? he says:
"It partakes of the portions of action and agent. This is the intended meaning:
In the expression *asaṃrabdhavān* (“not having been agitated”), there are two components: the action-component (*kriyāṃśa*) and the agent-component (*kārakāṃśa*).

Among these, when there is a negation of the meaning belonging to both components, the negation of the action-component occurs in the sentence due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), because that [action] is intended as the primary element to be expressed; thus, there is no failure to apprehend the predicate (*vidheyāvimarśa*) because it has not been left unstated.

Just as a compound is not desired in the case of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), so too, by the aforementioned principle, a compound is not desired in the case of relative negation (*paryudāsa*) either.
Thus he says: "Is it not well? Here, "not doing" (*na kurvatā*) means by one who is similar to an agent of the act of doing, yet is for all intents and purposes indifferent toward the action.
While one could simply say "not doing" (*akurvatā*), the expression "not doing" (*na kurvatā*) serves to negate the aspect of the action itself, as it produces a contrary understanding.
In this way, even though [the word] "not" is not [logically] appropriate, its negation of mere appropriateness results precisely in the opposite being understood.
The hearing of that [word "not"] is the hearing of the action.
The compound *tayoh* (of those two) is a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) whose meaning is already established.
A sentence has a meaning to be established.
Regarding the example "asūryampaśya" and so forth,
here too, the negative particle *nañ* does not have a direct connection with the word "sūrya," which is the subsequent member of the compound.
Rather, it is solely for the sake of the seer [of that action].

Even there, the agentive aspect is primary and not the aspect of the action; this is to be understood as before, because the suffix *khaś* is prescribed after a verbal root when the agent is intended.

For in the sentence "he eats" (*bhuṅkte*), the primacy of the action is perceived; however, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed in relation to an implied action such as "he is," the meaning of the sentence becomes "he is not one who eats at a funeral feast" (*śrāddhabhojī na bhavati*).

However, in the case of *aśrāddhabhojī*, since the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the agent of eating (*bhoktṛ*), one understands someone other than a "partaker of a śrāddha meal," namely, one who eats the remains (*vighasāśin*).
Since a negation is not intended here in compounds such as *aśrāddhabhojī*,

it is for this very reason that both the "compound of compatible meanings" (*samarthasamāsa*) and its opposite, the "compound of incompatible meanings" (*asamarthasamāsa*), have been explained by means of the two verses.
As for the distinction or non-distinction of sentences, their comprehension occurs through the force of the context; thus, no explicit statement is required.

Having thus examined this first instance of a failure to discern the predicate (*vidheya*), he cites a second example: "In the passage beginning with *yo 'sau*," because the expectancy toward the word *tat* (the correlative) is not resolved by anything [else].
Regarding the phrase "in one case": in some instances, there is an introduction with the relative pronoun *yat* followed by a conclusion with the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.
In some cases, it follows that there is an opening with the word *tat* and a conclusion with the word *yat*.
He will provide examples of these two according to the sequence of verbal opening and conclusion [in the following verse]:
"of those two also... (*tayor api*).

The word "api" (also/even) conjoins the meaning of the negative particle *na*. For it has been stated previously that in an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), the meaning of the negative particle is the thing to be enjoined and the object to be negated is the thing restated (*anuvādya*); whereas in an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the reverse is the case.
Regarding the phrase "the subject and the predicate":

although there is a constant syntactic connection between *yad* and *tad*, by the very nature of linguistic capacity (*śabdaśakti*), *yad* has the subject as its domain, while *tad* has the predicate as its domain.
This is because [this relationship] is eternal (*nityatvāt*).
Because it exists by virtue of having dependence as its life-force;
it is called "verbal" because both [the word and the object] are touched by the word;
the absence of such contact between both is "literal" (ārtha).
In this regard, there are two possibilities: the non-appropriation of one or the non-appropriation of both.
Even the non-appropriation of one is twofold, according to whether it serves as its basis;
this he will illustrate in due order.
It is "prepared" (*upakalpita*) because it is established through constant dependence;
and in this context, when the status of being an object of common renown (*prasiddha*) and so forth is indicated,
that which is "commonly renowned" (*sā kalā*) is so called because it is perceived with clarity.
In some instances, even that [demonstrative pronoun] is used as a designation, because it shares the same referent as the word *yat* (relative pronoun);
the meaning of "those" (*te*) is "which were experienced by me alone."
"He sought him" (anviyeṣa sa iti). Here, "him" (sa) means that which has been introduced [in the preceding context].

Regarding the phrase "the object already mentioned" (upāttavastu), the meaning is: by way of having as its object that thing which was mentioned in the verse to be cited later with the words "some person" (ko 'pi).

By means of this introduction and conclusion concerning the subject matter at hand, he demonstrates the subject matter to be excluded while clarifying the restriction on the over-extension of the application [of the rule] through the word "that" (tat):
"But that which is a single sentence... and so forth.
By the mention of "a single sentence," it is stated that the object being referred back appears as if directly perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇatā*).
Consequently, there is no fault in the division of sentences.
By the phrase "as the agent," it indicates predominance (*prādhānya*); this is for the purpose of making known that a reference to something non-predominant (*aprādhānya*) is not defective.
The word "sa" (he/that) refers to the object;
"tebhyaḥ" (from them) refers to the words beginning with "idam" (this), which denote agency;
and "asau" (that) refers to the pronoun "tat".

"Because of non-possession" (asamanvayāt) means that there is a contradiction regarding the relationship [between the word] and its object, since the word "that" (tat) denotes something imperceptible.
"For identity" (tādātmyāya) means for the sake of having the nature of Him whose crest is the digit of the moon.
The term "ārtha" (the object) indicates the sequence of the introduction and conclusion.

Regarding the phrase "kalpitatatkramādī" (the imagined sequence of that and so forth): the meaning of the word "yat" (that) is that which is designated by the pronoun; the sense is that its object—namely, the action (*karman*) and so forth—is imagined as being the object (*viṣaya*) in the form of the factors of action such as the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the meaning is that the sequence of that [action] and so forth is imagined.
Regarding the phrase "the twofold nature of the relation": the twofold nature arises from the distinction between the expressed (śābda) and the implied (ārtha).

As for the expression "yat-tat" (that which—this): when the word *tat* is employed in grammatical apposition with the word *yat*, it—by the very nature of the power of words—requires the word *yat* to have as its object a well-known entity (*prasiddha-vastu*).
However, when there is an indication through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) or mediation, it attains syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) with that which is specifically indicated.

For instance, in the passage, "Not only he who speaks ill of the great, but also he who hears from him shares in the sin," although the words *yaḥ* and *saḥ* are indicated in immediate succession and in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the connection is established with the specific term].

Nevertheless, according to the maxim "that which is powerful [does not depend on another]," if this word *tat* were employed here in dependence upon another word *yat* that is immediately preceding it,
then this fault would indeed arise; however,
since it is employed here with priority due to the intervention [of other words], it depends upon the word *yat* in the phrase *yaḥ* (rather than the immediately preceding one).

Since that [correlative *tat*] does not require another word, and by way of context it enters into a connection with the immediately preceding *yat* that has been indicated, it does not—by virtue of its prior grammatical impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*)—require another *tat*; thus, this is faultless.
In this manner, the two-fold sequence of the introduction and conclusion of *yat* and *tat* has been established.
And since that [objection] is not applicable here in this verse, he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

Regarding the phrase "in its appropriation" (*tadupādāne*): the word *yat* here refers back to the word *tat* which has been introduced; the meaning is that [the connection is established] through the cognition of their relationship.

Anticipating the objection that "the observation of actual usage itself will serve as the justification here," he states that usage may be caused by errors in recitation due to negligence, saying: "mīlitam" (closed).
"Tadabhinnārthaḥ" means having an object not different from the word "tat" (that);
[it refers to] "tasya," namely, the word "adaḥ" (this).
Regarding the case where the word *adaḥ* has a meaning non-different from that of the word *tat*, two faults have been stated.

First, when the word *adaḥ* is used alone—as in "asau marut" and so forth—there would be an expectancy for the word *yat*. Second, when the word *adaḥ* is used in conjunction with the word *yat*—as in "yo 'sau jagattraya" and so forth—there would be no expectancy for the previously employed word *tat*.

Here, the use of the word *yad* (which) devoid of the word *adaḥ* (that) is stated as an example; the meaning is that just as this [word *yad*] alone has a requirement for the word *tad* (it), so too does it when joined with the word *adaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "is postulated," the meaning is that in his view, the object—which is the thing as described through the uncontradicted traditional consensus (*prasiddhi*) of the learned—is impossible as something distinct from the referent of the word *tad*, because you assert that the word *adaḥ* possesses the same referent as the word *tad*, which would entail the necessity of referring back to the word *yad*.

"It is conceptualized" means that it is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because the validity of the stream of application would otherwise be inexplicable. In the phrase "without that," the word "that" refers to the stream of application.
The determination of whether something has that meaning or not is the determination of whether it is intended or unintended as its meaning.

However, if "her" (tām) were referred to, the identity of meaning with that [original object] would be untenable. One who follows what has already gone is called a "follower of the departed" (gatānugatika).
In this context, the suffix *ṭhan* has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
The meaning is: he who goes by that very same path by which one [other] goes, without any deliberation;
from that, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied.
"Non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*) involves the elision of the vowel *a* [from *vikalpa*];
the meaning is "without hesitation.
Alternatively, it means not by mere conceptualization (*vikalpamātra*).
Rather, the meaning is "directly.
*Smṛtibhū* means desire (*kāma*).
The second occurrence of the word *smṛtibhū* is used in the sense of an object of memory (*smaraṇa-viṣaya*).
The meaning is that because it has been burnt, only the memory remains; "from injury" means from killing;
"only of those separated [by time]" refers, for example, to passages such as "he who [perceives] without conceptualization," and so forth.
"Or when there is no intervention," as in *smṛtibhūḥ* and so forth.
It is for this very purpose that two examples have been stated.
In that context, "hi" refers to its usage accompanied by "idam" and so forth.
"Of those two" refers to "yat" and "tat.
"The other than that" means that when one is used arbitrarily, there is an expectation for the other.

It should be understood that the word *yad*, when employed in conjunction with "this" (*idam*) and so forth, naturally expects a corresponding *tad* whose mouth is opened [in anticipation], and likewise the word *tad* expects a *yad*.
This has been illustrated in sequence by the phrase "that which is this" (*yad etad*).

And regarding the phrase "so this": when it is intended to be demonstrated by means of another textual passage, the use of the word *tad* (that) is appropriate; however, in the present case, the word *yad* (which) has no connection with a previously introduced subject, nor is there recourse to the ellipsis of the word *tad* for the purpose of teaching the path of connection with a subject yet to be introduced.

And that which acts as a blemish upon good poetry must certainly be abandoned; specifically, when there is an uninterrupted usage of *yat* and *tat* in their midst without mentioning the referent to be understood between them— as in "that which is powerful" (*yat tad ūrjitam*) and so forth— then the repetition of those two, *yat* and *tat*, according to the requirements of the context,
is not faulty, as in "surely even that has been lost" (*nūnaṃ tad api hāritam*) and so forth.
Likewise, regarding those two, *yat* and *tat*:
when *idam* and the others are mentioned immediately following them, because *yat* and *tat* and those [words] beginning with *idam* remain joined together,
the mutual observation (*pratyavekṣā*) of *yat* and *tat* does not cease according to their respective application, just as it does not [cease] when *idam* and the others are not employed.
The meaning is that just as dependence does not cease when two things exist separately and independently, it remains even when they are joined together—
as in the cases of "that which is within the moon" and "this is the cloth."

Thus, in the present case as well, regarding the phrase "yo 'sāv" (he who is this), there are many distinctions: when the word *yat* is used in conjunction with *idam* and so forth separately, when the word *tat* is used in conjunction with *idam* and so forth separately, and when *yat* and *tat* are used in mutual conjunction.
Regarding the phrase "tatsāṅkarya" (their commingling): [the same applies].

There are many distinctions based on whether the word *yat* is used in conjunction with *idam* and so forth separately, whether the word *tat* is used in conjunction with *idam* and so forth separately, and whether *yat* and *tat* are used in mutual conjunction.
In these examples, only a mere indication has been shown.

Now, in connection with this topic, we shall examine the sequence of introduction and conclusion based on the constant correlation between *yad* and *tad*, which generally pervades the integration of the meaning of the sentence.
And that [repetition] is of three kinds, distinguished as *puṣṭa* (nourished), *apuṣṭa* (unnourished), and *duṣṭa* (defective).
Even the *puṣṭa* type is first of two kinds, distinguished as being verbal (*śābda*) or non-verbal (*ārtha*).
The verbal type is also of two kinds: that which begins with the word *yad* and that which begins with the word *tad*.

The correlative (*ārtha*) [demonstrative] is also threefold when the relative pronoun *yad* is not employed: because the employed demonstrative *tad* is connected with an object that is well-known, previously experienced, or under current discussion.

The relative pronoun *yad*, when the demonstrative *tad* is not employed, is twofold: because the relative alone is connected with an object under current discussion or with an object consisting of an imagined action and so forth.
However, when neither is employed, there is only one variety, based on the assumption that both have as their object a thing already presented.
Thus, the sequence of introduction and conclusion for *yad* and *tad* is eightfold—twofold verbal and sixfold objective—and is well-established.
This very [sequence] has been illustrated here by the author of the treatise.

However, in cases such as "that which is powerful" (*yat tad ūrjitam*), there is a commingling of the verbal and objective sequences of conclusion; therefore, this does not constitute a separate category.
Since the "deficient" (apuṣṭa) will be described in the context of the "corrupt" (duṣṭa), the "corrupt" is now being analyzed.

In that regard, when the pronouns *tat* and *yat* are used in immediate succession with words such as *idam* and so forth—either through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or by substituting for *tat* and *yat*—there is indeed a defect, because those [words] do not have that [referent] as their meaning. An example used in proximity to them is:
"yo 'sau kutra camatkṛteḥ" ("That which is there, where is its wonder?").
In this way, examples such as "this" (*idam*) and so forth should be inferred by means of the accompaniment of the word "that" (*tat*).

Whether they are used in a remote sense, a proximate sense, or with grammatical disagreement (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), there is neither fault nor lack of fault; rather, there is simply a lack of nourishment (*apuṣṭatva*). For example, in the phrase "yo 'vikalpam" [from the *Smṛticandrikā*], the term "smṛtibhūḥ" is repeated.
Thus, this has been illustrated by beginning with the word *tat* (that).

Likewise, because the word *tat* refers back to an object that is not currently present to the senses, it is defective when used to refer back to a principal object that is directly perceived and situated within the same sentence;
as, for example, in "May he whose crest is the digit of the moon [protect] you," and so forth.

By the mention of the "principal," not merely the agent is indicated; rather, another factor of action (kāraka) is also intended as being primary and thus appearing as if directly perceived. Therefore:
having conquered the earth, which has the four oceans for its girdle...
Having entrusted the burden of state affairs to his ministers, he remained there at his ease.
Thus, they say that Medinī’s reference by means of the word *tat* (that) is not elegant.

For example, when the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat* exist in two distinct states—one residing in the meaning of a single word (*padārtha*) and the other having the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)—then, because their objects are different, this constitutes a flaw that obstructs their necessary connection. As for instance: [Example omitted per instructions] In such cases, the relationship is inherently defective due to the disparity in their referents.
Where now are those hundreds of gold coins or those herds of rutting elephants that Śrī Harṣa bestowed upon the virtuous Bāṇa?
But as for the fame that Bāṇa carved out for him with the profusion of his elegant compositions, I believe it does not suffer even the slightest fading, even at the dissolution of the eon.

Thus: the word *yā* [in the example] has as its object the meaning of a single word (*padārtha*), whereas the pronoun *tat* [in the example] has as its object the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). If it were to have the meaning of a single word as its object, it would be *tā*.

In this very context, regarding the readings "yad bāṇena tu tasya" and "tāḥ kalpapralaye 'pi," if the former refers to the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) and the latter is established upon the meaning of the word (*padārtha*), then an example should be provided accordingly.

Therefore, one should read it as "yā bāṇena tu" and "tāḥ kalpapralaye 'pi. However, in this case [the following is an example]: "The blue lotus, by its resemblance to the flax flower; the ketaka, by its conformity to the withered birch leaf..."
And if you think that the *vakula* tree functions like a *karavīra*, then, O bee, alas, the loss will be yours alone.
Thus, it is not only the word *yad* that refers to the meaning of the sentence, but the word *tad* as well; provided, however,
that this sentence-meaning has been condensed by the word *hāni* and made manifest, and is then referred to by the word *tad*.
For this very reason, the feminine gender of the word *tat* here is employed with the intention of referring to the object being predicated (*vidheya*),
whereas *tat sāmpratam* is used with the intention of referring to that which is already established (*anuvādya*).
In both cases, the adoption of the gender is established by the tradition of the learned.

Furthermore, because the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat* are invariably connected, and because a subordinate element (*guṇa*) and a principal element (*pradhāna*) are fit to be related, [the former] is referred to when it has been pointed out in one sentence containing the word *yat* or in a sentence containing the word *tat*;
or else, when it is subsequently recalled,
it is done so by another word *yat* pointed out in the sentence containing the first *yat*, due to the mutual connection between the subordinate and principal elements.
And thus, when there is such a misconception (*parāmarśa*), there are two types of faulty non-difference (*duṣṭābheda*). For example:

"By whom those rivers of ichor from the elephants of the Thirty-three [gods] were drunk with the heat of their prowess; by whom pleasure-drinking grounds were fashioned in the shade of the trees of Nandana; and by whom the roars of the night-stalkers caused the agitation of the city of the gods—what has been done by them that is worthy of praise, or what has been performed that brings you satisfaction? [In this verse, the non-difference between the subject and the object of the comparison is faulty.]
Thus: the word *kṣapācāriṇām* (of the night-walkers), ending in the genitive case, is connected with the word *yat* and is subsequently referred to by another word *yat*.
The reading *kṣapācāribhiḥ* (by the night-walkers) is more logical.
In this way, that which is indicated in a sentence containing the word *tat* is not defective when it is referred to by words *yat*, as for example:

Victorious everywhere are those of wondrous intellect, such as Bhartṛmeṇḍa and others, whose playful mastery of speech is so adept at plundering the state of aesthetic relish— that juice renowned in the thick, pale center of a fully ripened Puṇḍra sugarcane, and that which is found in the sweet-tart fruit of the royal jambū tree.
Thus [it is said]. Here, in the second *yacchabda* sentence, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which is to be referred to is indicated and is then referred to by the word *tat*.
However, in the first *yacchabda* sentence, a reference by the word *yat* is not appropriate because there is no connection between the two, as in:
"Homage be to them; they triumph in the world—those [stars] that shed nectar, and those utterances of the lords of poets."
The life-story of the wielder of the Pināka bow reaches a state where only existence remains, having severed all other worldly attachments.
Thus, it is not proper to refer back, by means of another word "that" (*tat*), to the words of the masters of poets that have been indicated by a sentence containing the word "that.

Furthermore, since the words "what" (*yat*) and "that" (*tat*) by their very nature give rise to a split in the sentence, if one of these two words is used in one sentence while the other is used [in another], that too is indeed defective. For example:
"And yet there is no hope for me, who am captivated by the extraordinary and most wonderful deeds of the Uncommon One that have been witnessed..."
This is some being in the form of a heroic child, a reality consisting of a sublime surge of the essence of immeasurable majesty.
In this context, the phrase "even though" (*yady api*) is required;
however, it is not fit to be connected within that single sentence.

For even within a single sentence, when the pronoun *tat* (that) is employed with reference to a subject under discussion, it may do so by relying on an imagined distinction residing in qualities, actions, and so forth.

Since that which is to be referred to in the principal action is indeed primary, it is proper to mention it by its own form; however, when it concerns a subordinate action and so forth, it is only proper to refer to it by means of a pronoun. Any deviation from this is certainly defective. For example:
"For the sake of the prosperity of his subjects alone, he took tribute from them. [In this case, the reference to the subjects should have been made by their own name rather than by a pronoun.]
For the sun indeed takes up its essence in order to emit it a thousandfold.
Thus, the correct reading is: "He took tribute from his subjects for their very prosperity.

Likewise, when there is a single subject [for the correlative pronouns], it is indeed defective if one of the two—*yat* or *tat*—refers to a substance and so forth, while the other has time or the like as its scope. For example:
"You are thus possessed of beauty, and he is the familiar abode of loveliness; here, you two alone attain the ultimate limit of the arts."
O fortunate one! By good fortune, that pair corresponds;
from this point on, whatever remains shall be won by you, now multiplied.

In this context, one should read "if there were a remainder" (*ataḥ śeṣaṃ cet syāt*), because the word *cet* has the meaning of "if" (*yadi*). Likewise, once it is established that the pronoun *tat* refers to what has been previously introduced, it is indeed a fault for it to have as its scope a thing that is about to be introduced. For example: "For those whose minds are awakened by the happiness of contentment, pride is not different [from them]; and for those men whose intellects are crowded with greed for wealth, [pride] is far away."
For whose sake was such a place of abundance created by Fate? Mount Meru, whose golden glory is fully realized within itself alone, does not please me.
In this context, Meru, being the subject under discussion, is referred to by the pronoun "sa" (he/that). This is an example of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
However, in a single sentence (*ekavākya*), it is as follows:

"By means of the Ganges flowing upstream at his sacred ford due to the construction of an elephant-bridge"—thus it should be given. Likewise, it is certainly faulty when there is a reference by another [word] with repetition (*savīpsa*) after an initial mention by one [word] without repetition (*nirvīpsa*). For example:
"Whoever is excluded from auspiciousness, he, each one, experiences misfortune."

However, when there is a conclusion with a non-repetitive [word] following a single step that was repetitive, because the repetitive element has been withdrawn, there is no faulty connection; rather, it is simply "unsubstantial" (apuṣṭa). For example:
"You are the lord of auspicious splendors; you ordain holy fortune here; O God, bestow it upon me for long! Be gracious!

Whatever [evil] I have committed, O Lord of the World, abandon it all! In this case, although the word *yat* is repeated, the repetition is not faulty because the concluding *yad* (in *yad yat*) refers back to the preceding *yat* as a whole. However, the lack of a corresponding *tat* at the end renders the construction unsubstantial. Thus, while the connection is not defective, the poetic merit is lacking.
To me, who am bowed before you— may it be well with you— grant me, O Blessed One,
that which is auspicious for the sake of my greatest welfare.
Thus [it is said]. Here, whatever is indicated by "yad yad" (whatever... whatever) is referred to by the word "tat" alone.

This is an example of the relative pronoun *yacchabda* with repetition (*savīpsa*). However, an example of the word *tacchabda* with repetition being referred to by a non-repetitive form is as follows:

We have practiced forbearance, yet not out of true patience; we have abandoned the comforts suited to a home, yet not through contentment; we have endured the unbearable afflictions of cold, wind, and heat, yet not performed true austerity; we have meditated day and night with restrained breaths, yet not upon the state of Śambhu. We have performed those very same deeds as the sages, yet we have been deprived of their respective fruits.

Thus [it is said]. However, where there is a reference by means of a distributive term (*savīpsa*) following an initial introduction with a distributive term, there indeed exists "fullness" (*puṣṭatva*); for example:
"Whosoever bears a weapon, heavy upon his own arm; whosoever among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas—be he a child of the Pañcāla lineage, or one of advanced age, or even one still in the womb;

whosoever is a witness to those deeds and moves against me in battle; and whosoever is ablaze and blinded by rage—of each and every one of them, I am myself the end-maker, even of the End-maker of the worlds."

Thus [it is said]. And where there is a reflective reference (*pratyavamarśa*) by means of multiple [words] to that which is multiple and accompanied by distributive repetition (*savīpsa*), there too there is indeed fullness (*puṣṭatva*). For example:
"Whichever limb-by-limb portion he might obtain, touching it with his hand, in each case he considers only that much alone to be your supreme form."
Alas, O Lord of Elephants, you have been led by cruel fate to that city of those born blind! Indeed, what person in this world could possibly be a knower of the majesty of the entire universe?

Thus [it is argued]: if, at the outset, one says "whichever... whichever," and in the subsequent reflection one says "only that much," there would be a failure to reflect upon the predicate because the distributive sense of that meaning is subordinated within the compound.
This is not so;
for by the inclusion of the word *mātra*, restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is expressed, as in the rule: "in the mere [expression of] the meaning of the nominal stem, gender, measure, and number."

And since that [compound] is dependent upon what is being determined (*avadhāryamāṇa-paratantra*), the primacy of the object of determination itself—being accompanied by *vīpsā* (repetition)—remains entirely unimpaired due to its predominance.
In some cases, a *sup-supā* compound is observed based on the predominance of the prior member's meaning, as for example:
"Then his vigor, which was almost extinguished, seemed to be rekindled by the excellence of his body."
Followed by the two forest deities, the daughter of the king of mountains came into view.
Thus, in the compound *nirvāṇabhūyiṣṭham* ("abounding in nirvāṇa"), the meaning of *nirvāṇa* alone is predominant because it stands as the qualifier of *vīrya*.

However, in this case [of *tanmātrakam*], the meaning of that [suffix] will not be predominant in such a way. Now, when the word *mātra* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), for what purpose is the suffix *-ka* employed?
Or, even if that [particle *eva*] were used, for what purpose would the word *eva* be there?
Or rather, why is the word *eva* itself not employed?
This is not so.

In this context, since the suffix -ka conveys a sense of contempt (*kutsā*), there is no tautology. When the word *eva* is used alone—as in "that very thing" (*tam eva*)—its meaning is perceived as if scattered;
however, when the term *mātra* is employed, its meaning is perceived as a single, unified whole. Thus, there is a distinction between the two.
If, at most, the mention of both [terms] is for the purpose of establishing a restriction by following worldly convention—
for such usage of two restrictive expressions is indeed observed in cases like this:
"The child merely weeps with tears whose shimmering water flows down."
In this very case, when "that" (*tat*) is indicated without repetition (*nirvīpsena*) and the city of those born blind (*jātyandhapura*) is subsequently referred to without repetition,
then there is no fault whatsoever because the reference is appropriate.
Likewise, where the word "which" (*yat*) is indicated in the preceding sentence but the word "that" (*tat*) is not indicated in the subsequent sentence, [the same principle applies].
In that regard, it is indeed defective because of its expectancy, as in:
"That which was done by the lotuses toward the moon, which excels in loveliness, is [only] fitting when it is closed.
However, there is no defect when the word *yat* is employed within the subsequent sentence and the word *tat* is employed in the preceding sentence.
Rather, it is the very excellence (*puṣṭatva*) previously established that is intended here, because it is introduced generally and subsequently particularized.
With this intention in mind, it was stated that [the figure] has as its object things such as actions that are merely imagined (*kalpita*).

An example is the following, where the order of the two halves of the preceding verse is reversed: "By the lotuses, a service was rendered to the moon, which is already preeminent in beauty, in that they were closed [by it]."

Although the relative pronoun *yad* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat* are indistinguishable in their function as referents, the word *yad* mentioned in the subsequent sentence refers to the object by its very nature through proximity (*āvidūrya*), because it is not detached from the meaning of the preceding sentence;

the word *tat*, however, does so through remoteness (*vaidūrya*), because it is fixed upon an object that appears as remote. Furthermore, this proximity, by bringing excellence to the subject matter at hand, unifies the meanings of the two sentences.
And thus, when the object is already established in such a way that it is fit for the use of the pronoun *yad*, the employment of the pronoun *tad* is indeed redundant.

"Seeing that beauty of her two curved eyebrows, which was as if fashioned by a stick of collyrium and was so skillful in its playfulness, the Bodiless One (Kāma) abandoned the pride in the beauty of his own bow."
In this context, the words *yām* and *yat*, which appear at the beginning of the verse, should be read in reverse order. For example:
"Her gaze does not rain nectar; her face does not exude honey-like smiles; her heart is not moist with tenderness; nor are her limbs touched by sandalwood paste.
Upon whom has this cruel, burning fire found its footing? Surely it is some other fire, made of adamant, for such is its behavior."
In this context, "yasya" (of whom) should be read [instead of "yena"]. And as it is said:
"That Blessed One is indeed my teacher, his name being the one we are to accept; therefore, through his grace, I am capable of this secret doctrine of the bow.
Seated here, how is it that I—oh!—must string the bow that was made the wager for Sītā’s hand in marriage, the very path of the forest-dwellers?"

And here, since it should be read as "this is the Upaniṣad of the bow," so too, regarding what was previously stated— "hundreds of bhāras of gold"— it should be read thus: "I believe those glories of his, which were engraved by Bāṇa through the profusion of his compositions, do not undergo even the slightest fading even at the dissolution of the aeon."

Furthermore, when the object to be referred back is not explicitly stated, and the sentence begins with the word *yad* (which), while the subsequent mention containing *tat* refers to that same object, there arises a cognition that hovers over the preceding sentence-meaning without touching the object to be referred back; because this results in a remoteness from the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, it constitutes a lack of reinforcement (*apuṣṭatva*). For example:
"That which, having risen upon being struck by the foot, climbs onto the head..."
For an embodied being in good health, it is better that passion arise from an insult than [to suffer] from [the loss of] one's own state.
For this very reason, if the two half-verses were transposed here, there would indeed be "plenitude" (puṣṭatva).

Likewise, when it is proper to refer to a meaning already indicated in the sense of a preceding sentence by means of a pronoun alone in the sense of a subsequent sentence, the employment of a pronoun accompanied by its own specific word is certainly faulty. For example:

"The earth is bounded by the ocean, and that reservoir of waters extends but a hundred yojanas; Pūṣan is ever a traveler across the measure of the sky"—such is generally the state of mind, constrained by the seal of perceived limits. But this unfolding of wisdom belonging to the virtuous, on the other hand, triumphs as being truly limitless.
Thus [it is said]. Here, in the phrase "and that treasure of waters," the word *sasva* is a reference using a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
Likewise, it should be understood that in the phrase "in those certain [places] on that mountain" (*tasminn adrau kati cid*), the context is the hermitages of Rāmagiri.
However, some here justify this by stating that in the compound "Rāmagiri-āśramaiḥ" (in the hermitages of Rāmagiri), Rāmagiri has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

Since [the subject] does not appear with intensity in the *buddhi*, how can it be referred to by a pronoun? Regarding the question of how there can be a connection with a pronoun for that which is concealed by the function (*vṛtti*), it is established on the intention of referring to that which has become the primary [subject], as in: "The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge";
thus, that [knowledge] is what is being explained.
In this context, the mention of "on the mountain" (*adrāv*) would, by conveying the mere notion of a mountain, fail to indicate the specific mountain under discussion.

Therefore, both [the mountain and its specific name] must be included here, just as in the case of [Patañjali’s opening]: "Now, the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*), followed by "Of which words? (*keṣāṃ śabdānām*).

In the case of the word *giri*, since "mountain" (*adri*) was introduced by the word *giri* and then [referred to] by another synonym, the resulting inconsistency is indeed difficult to avoid. However, in the phrase "the earth bounded by the ocean" (*udanvacchinnā bhūḥ*), because the ocean (*udanvat*) is proximate and appropriate, and because the earth cannot be referred to by the pronoun *saḥ* due to its feminine gender, a reference by means of a pronoun is indeed more suitable.
Furthermore, [the claim] that it is not within the scope of its own word is itself faulty.
Moreover, when a certain aggregate is designated by a particular sentence,

and another sentence must then perform a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of a member of that aggregate, one must designate that aggregate with the pronoun *ya-* (the relative "who/which") so that the object of the selection may be understood.
The specification of a constituent part that is being singled out is indeed faulty. For example:
"From him was born Manu, the seed of the nine kings, in whose lineage were both Sagara and Bhagīratha;

by the one, this ocean was made into a moat, and by the other, it was filled with the river of the Siddhas. In this case, the specific part being singled out is "the one" (*yena*) and "the other" (*anyena*), yet the verse fails to specify which is which, resulting in a lack of clarity.
In this context, regarding what was indicated by the words "that Sagara" and "that Bhagīratha," a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) has been prescribed by means of the word "one" (*eka*) and so forth.
Selection is the separation of a single member from a group on the basis of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*).
However, in this case, no group has been indicated by any word.
And that which is indicated by the term "by one" is not a whole collection, but rather a single part.
Consequently, there is a fault here because of the indication of what is both indicatable and non-indicatable, as well as the indication of what is non-indicatable and indicatable.

Thus, since it is the collective whole that is the object of specification and must be indicated by the word *yat*, the reading "one [of them] buried the oceans, while the second showered them with the waters of the Gaṅgās" is superior.

In some cases, when the meaning of a sentence is being presented through the relationship of injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), there is a defect if the *yat* and *tat* pronouns are omitted or if their order is otherwise altered. For example:
"That lotus which has a luster equal to your eye is submerged in the water.
Here, in the first and third quarters [of the verse], there is a composition based on the relationship of injunction and restatement by means of the employment of the *yat* and *tat* pronouns.
The transgression of that [rule] is a fault because it occurs in the second quarter [of the verse].

Since blue lotuses (*indīvara*) and royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*) are numerous, the adoption of the relationship between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the restatement (*anuvāda*) is for the purpose of distinguishing the blue lotus and the royal swan—which are compared to objects related to Sītā—from other instances.
However, some maintain that this is not done for the moon because it is singular.
That is incorrect;

for since even the moon can be manifold through distinctions such as a second moon and so forth, the relationship of injunction and restatement (vidhi-anuvāda) would likewise be appropriate there. In the case of blue lotuses, however, there is a primary distinction due to the difference between individual instances.
If it is argued that for the moon, which is of a single manifested form, its diversity due to differences in time and differences in state is merely secondary, we say no;
for the manifestations of the moon are indeed distinct,
for one moon is that of the second day, and another is the full moon.
And for this very reason, the qualification "resembling the luster of the face" is provided in order to convey the perception of a full moon by excluding [the image] from being like a second moon;
for the word *śaśin* does not denote a full moon, since it signifies the moon in general.
If it is argued that in numerical conventions there is a cognition of the moon as being one, [we reply:
in certain linguistic usages regarding universals (*jāti*), the oneness of blue lotuses and the like is also established.

Therefore, since in poetic usage multiplicity is treated as residing in the moon, it is preferable here to maintain the relationship of injunction and restatement (*vidhi-anuvāda-bhāva*) based upon that [multiplicity].
Furthermore, placing that word (*tat*) in an inappropriate position serves only to distance its comprehension, as in:
"Walk with a soft step; the ground is covered in darbha grass; place the hem of your garment upon your head; the heat is fierce.

Here, in the phrase "place the hem of your garment," the word *tat* (meaning "therefore") should have been placed at the beginning of the third line as a causal particle (*hetvartha*), yet it is misplaced.
And there, its employment serves no purpose;
for it produces a dullness of comprehension regarding that [object].
In some cases, the verbal mention by its own name of a subordinate action—which has already been referred to by a pronoun such as *tad* in relation to the principal action—is indeed faulty.
Regarding the phrase "as in the nearby sky":
here, does the pronoun *tasmai* refer back to the cloud previously introduced, or does it refer to the *jīmūta* (cloud) mentioned within this very verse?

In the first case, the mention of *jīmūta* would be redundant; for in the principal action, it is the previously introduced cloud—already referred to—that is logically capable of being connected with the sense of the sentence.
For it is not the case that for as many things as there is a connection with something, each one of them is individually specified;
what is established in one place is relied upon elsewhere through expectancy and so forth.
Therefore, the mention of "cloud" (*jīmūta*) need not be made.
On the contrary, such a construction produces the cognition of a different entity and brings about a sense of distaste.
Now, if it is argued that by the word *tat* (that), the cloud occurring in this verse is referred back [to the previous context],
that is incorrect.

Since throughout this entire section the reference remains fixed solely to the cloud previously introduced, it is logical that the reference here should likewise be to that same cloud; thus, the repeated mention of *jīmūta* (cloud) is indeed purposeless. Having thus analyzed the second instance of the failure to identify the predicate (*vidheya*), he begins to elaborate upon the third instance within this very verse, starting with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).

By the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*), it is established in another manner that there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) [in the case of *dvandva*] because it expresses simultaneous action, with the exception of *dvandva*.

Among those, regarding the first [type], it is a *tatpuruṣa* because of the statement: "A *karmadhāraya* is a *tatpuruṣa* with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Because of the statement: "A *bahuvrīhi* consists of [words] with a common substratum," a *bahuvrīhi* generally has as its domain only those things with a common substratum.
However, in cases such as *susūkṣmajaṭakeśa* ("one whose matted hair is very fine"), it is accepted even for words that have different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*),
provided they refer to the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in that very instance;
this is because of the rule stating "when [it concerns] number," whereby a *dvigu* compound is defined as one preceded by a numeral, even when it is *vyadhikaraṇa*.
The word "of the negation" (*pratiṣedhasya*) refers to the negative particle *nañ*, because of the commencement of the rule concerning *nañ*.
The word "second" (*dvitīya*) is used in a different grammatical case (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The word "of the factors of action" (*kārakāṇām*) is [explained] by such rules as "the agent and the instrument are frequently compounded with a *kṛt*-suffix."
The genitive case in the phrase "of the relation" (*saṃbandhasya*) and so forth [indicates that the relation belongs to the compound].
In that context as well—that is, when there is a connection with a case-role (*kāraka*) or a relation—examples such as *adhistri* ("with regard to a woman") and *upakumbham* ("near the jar") occur.
The "own locus" (*svāśraya*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

"Vidheyadhurām" means the level or the actual state of being the object of prescription (vidheya) of that which is the object of prescription according to the function of words; the meaning is "by way of its actual status as the object of prescription.
"By way of being similar to what is being restated" (anūdyamānakalpatayā) means by way of actual predominance, without regard for the verbal predominance.
The meaning is that [the word] would cease to exist because, due to the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), it is no longer perceived as being distinct [from its components].
"In one case" refers to when it contains both the predicate and the subject;
"in the other case" refers to when it merely indicates a relationship.

The meaning is that one may distinguish [the cases] because the *Mahāvibhāṣā* is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a fixed or restricted option). "Of the very same" refers to the predominance residing in the qualifier and the non-predominance residing in the other [the qualified] which belongs to that very same [qualifier].

Regarding the phrases "for one" and "but for another," the word "fruit" (phala), which was introduced in the context of "herein is the difference in fruit," should be connected [to these two clauses].
Here, an objection is raised: "Since it is not established that contradiction resides in both entities, [your] statement regarding its absence here is incorrect.
That is not so;
for contradiction, characterized by non-coexistence, is not the only type of contradiction residing in entities; there is also difference (*bheda*)."

That which has acquired its functional manifestation in cold, heat, and so forth—what then? There is also a second type of contradiction characterized by existing through mutual exclusion, based on the categories of "entity" (vastu) and "non-entity" (avastu).
For in that case, if contradiction based on an entity is not possible, why should contradiction based on an entity and a non-entity not be possible?
And for this reason, it was stated during the stage of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that [the contradiction] exists only between existence and non-existence.
This is not a fault,
because the contradiction, which rests upon a real entity and its absence, functions to negate their identity (tādātmya).
If indeed there were primacy, then within that very same category there could be no non-primacy for itself, or if there were non-primacy, there could be no primacy.
Furthermore, how could there not be a lack of predominance for that which is predominant in one respect, given another perspective?
It would not be so only if both were real entities like cold and heat;
but this is not the case here, because what is merely intended by the speaker lacks ontological reality.
Just as in the case of "the king's man," where the king's primacy is merely intended (vaivakṣika) while his actual (vāstavam) status is indeed one of non-primacy, so too should it be understood here.
Thus, the summary meaning (piṇḍārtha) here is this: a negation of conjunction (saṃsarga) must be made;
and since that [conjunction] resides in two entities, there can be no negation of one thing in the other due to the absence of both here.
"By another" means by that which expresses the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
Regarding "mutually":

although it has been stated that for mutual qualifiers there is a compound only with the qualified object—according to the rule "a qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified object"—[nevertheless...]

Nevertheless, in the case of "one-eyed and lame" (*kāṇakhañja*) and so forth, the compound of mutually qualifying attributes has been established by relying on the intention to express one as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), based on the statement that "the qualifier and the qualified may be used according to one's wish. With that intent, there is the possibility of a mutual [qualification], expressed by the word "mutually" (*anyonya*).
In the expression *dārasukha*, it should be analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the pleasure of wives" (*dārāṇāṃ sukham*).

If it were a *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *ṭac* would not apply according to the rule *rājāhassakhibhyaṣ ṭac*. [This is illustrated by the vocative] "O King" (*he rājan*), "O Day" (*he ahan*), and "O Friend" (*he sakhe*).
In the case of *mṛtasya śiśor dvijasya*, a compound is suspected;
however, *rāmasya pāṇir asi* is an example of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Here, in some instances a compound of nominative agents and objects is suspected, in others of genitive possessors and objects, and in yet others of vocatives.
"By the method to be explained" refers to the investigations such as "Vyāsa is the son of Parāśara" and so forth.
"The preceptor of archery" [refers to Droṇa].
For here, by way of restating [the Lord’s] victory over Tripura and so forth, there is the injunction of his being the preceptor of archery and so on;
and the matter being restated is perceived as bringing about the excellence of that which is enjoined.
Yet this is not the case, because the *indravajrā* meter has been employed in place of the *upendravajrā*.
"We have approached [it]"—
even the harshness of sound (*duḥśravatva*) in a verse is simply an impropriety of words,
as those who speak of it do, comparing it to the lack of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and so forth.

In this context, the passage beginning with "Just as in the quality of the cause" (*yathā ca kāraṇaguṇe*) and ending with the intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*) fits coherently when read before the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) "Just as he [was] tender with compassion" (*yathā taṃ kṛpāmṛdu*). Furthermore, the section on examples (*udāharaṇa*) would likewise be consistent if followed by the counter-example;
indeed, such a reading is observed in the manuscripts.
Therefore, one must remain vigilant in this matter.
Parāśara and Jamadagni are the authorities here;
the word "cause" (hetu) is used in a compound with the pronoun "that" (tat), referring back to those two as the reason for their absence.
Furthermore, in this context, the mention of the term "Pārāśarya" (the son of Parāśara) and so forth regarding Vyāsa and others is redundant, as it merely conveys excellence (*utkarṣa*).

In the expression "the serpent Takṣaka," since the specific nature of the serpent is already understood from the word "Takṣaka" itself, the word "serpent" (*sarpa*) is intended solely to convey excellence; thus, its meaning is that which is to be predicated (*vidheya*).

Just as in the phrase "the red Takṣaka," the genus "serpent" is understood from the word "Takṣaka" alone, so too the quality characterized by "redness" is understood from that very same word, as it is invariably concomitant with it.
Therefore, those two—birth and quality—are stated with the intention of being the objects to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and they must not be subordinated within a compound.

The meaning is that, according to the logic already stated, because they are the objects to be enjoined, a compound does not occur. Furthermore, there is no other alternative when that [compound] is excluded.
Here two alternatives have been set forth: either the mere description of Takṣaka’s own nature, or the injunction of a quality called "red.
An investigation has been conducted regarding both of these;
and the meaning of "in its absence" (tadatyaye) is that there is no third alternative beyond the two positions already mentioned.
Having thus analyzed the *karmadhāraya* compound up to this point, he speaks regarding the determination of the *bahuvrīhi*: "In the *bahuvrīhi*, as follows.

Thereby, the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to those [factors] such as the preparation of the site (*sthalīkaraṇa*) which were previously mentioned as qualifiers; by means of those [factors], namely the injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth.
The non-perception of that refers to the non-perception of excellence or deficiency.
This occurs when there is a cause for a difference in perception regarding the use of compounds or non-compounds,
and regarding the capacity for comprehension in the domain of *karmadhāraya* and other types of compounds.
The impossibility of that [effect] is the impossibility of a difference in cognition;
the meaning is that the production of the effect is indeed logical when the causes have reached their final state.
He states the contradiction with observed fact regarding the acceptance of this [position].
"Thus indeed," or "or rather not at all," because there is no difference in the underlying logic (*nyāya*).

Furthermore, regarding the term *ardhajaratīyam*, it is derived from the compound *ardhaṃ jaratyāḥ* (half of an old woman), and the suffix *cha* is applied to indicate that which pertains to that [subject].
The meaning is: "just as an old woman desires the private parts but does not desire the face, so it is exactly like that.
"Tat tasya" means "that of his"; "tat" means "therefore";
"tau" refers to the sun and the moon.
The phrase "of those two" refers to the Sun and Moon as the subjects of the statement (*anuvādya*).
The expression "by way of succession" indicates their status as the objects to be enjoined (*vidheya*) through the medium of being grandfathers.
For this very reason, the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the form "the Sun and Moon" reveals the rivalry between the two.

The absence of a compound in the phrase "by Urvaśī and by Bhū" is for the purpose of demonstrating the primary and secondary status of the marriage; for while one [the marriage to Urvaśī] is real, the other is produced by the poet’s bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*).
Here, the variety of perception in the word "and" (*ca*) is indeed quite clear; let the wise man grasp this, so that Janaka may be connected with the subsequent [line].
In this context, the royal sages named Janaka and others attribute excellence to their status as fathers and so forth.
Having thus analyzed the *bahuvrīhi* compound, he explains the *dvigu* with the words "as in the case of *dvigu*.
[In the phrase] "without remainder" (*niravaśeṣa*), the number seven is the locus of emphasis because it is that which is to be predicated; however, in the compound, it is subordinated.

In the phrase "in ten" (*daśasu*), the fact that the number ten is what is to be predicated reveals the extreme degree of Rāvaṇa’s humiliation: even placing one's foot upon a single head is a cause for humiliation, how much more so when it is upon ten?
Thus;
the counter-example is found here in the reading "yasya sa" and so forth within the *saptāṅgī*,
where "vaiśasam" means affliction (*bādha*).
Having thus explained the double negative (*dvigu*), he explains the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) with the words "nañsamāse.

Regarding the phrase "it was shown," in the analysis of the predicate in the expression "he did not exert himself" (*asaṃrabdhavān*), one should state either "he did not speak" (*anuktavān*) or "he did not say" (*noktavān*).

Then, with the words beginning with "deśa," he provides examples in sequence for the six grammatical relations (kārakas), such as the agent (*kartṛ*), and for their connection within a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Regarding the phrase "so 'yam" (this is that), the explanation here is "this is indeed that. [The weapons] belonging to those who cause harm are *ghasmarāṇi*, meaning they have the nature of devouring (*grasana-śīla*); for this very reason, they are heavy (*gurūṇi*).
"Karaṇam" means depending upon the action;
"tat tasya" refers to that which has been introduced as the qualificand, namely the instrument;
"tasya" refers to Rāma.
"Valour" means strength;
"subordinate" (nighna) means dependent on another.
By that [word], namely "by Rāma," it serves as a qualification.
Regarding the phrase "of many" (*anekeṣām*):
since the word *aneka* is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), there would follow the use of the singular number because the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant.

This is true; however, in the domain of the usage of the negative particle, the word *eka* refers to things other than one, just as in the case of *abrāhmaṇa*, where the word *brāhmaṇa* has as its referent those belonging to the kṣatriya and other classes.
Furthermore, a single distinct entity is sometimes perceived as colored by oneness, and sometimes by its own intrinsic nature alone.
In the first case, it becomes "the manifold" (*aneka*); in the second, however, it becomes "the many" (*anekāni*).
And as Patañjali states in the *Padamañjarī*: "The mind is the single instigator (*prayojaka*) of the diverse activities of many.
The term *gurudattam* should be explained as "given by the Guru.
The phrase *tat tasyāḥ* means [the action] belonging to her—that is, the act of going whose agent is Sītā, who functions as the qualifier.

"for the sake of the teacher" (*gurvartham*) means "this is for the teacher"; this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Adverbial modifiers take the neuter gender and function as the direct object (*karman*).
If, however, they were intended as the most desired object (*īpsitatama*), the genitive case would be required.
"By way of purposeful activity" is stated because of the concluding remark, "he seeks it.
"That for him" is the qualification "that which is for the sake of the teacher";
[it refers to] that [gift] of the seeker.
"Being despised" means being undesirable;
"being despised" means being censured.
"As if no different from his own daughter" means:
It is indeed an adverbial modifier.

In the phrase "the act of circumambulation" (*pradakṣiṇakriyā*), the act of circumambulation—which serves as the object for the act of passing by—is primary because it is the instrumental cause for the obstacle. Likewise, in the phrase "first awakened," primacy is [primary].
The same should be understood regarding [the qualities of] being according to desire and being according to time.
By the phrase "that which is beheld," the excellence of physical form (*rūpasampat*) is indicated;
by the phrase "with one's own hand," the instrument (*karaṇa*) is expressed.

Regarding the phrase "written by one's own hand" (*svahastalikhita*): although the word *svahasta* (one's own hand) serves as a cause for conveying respect and is thus a ground for excellence with respect to the act of writing, it has been subordinated within the compound.
The expression "as before" (*pūrvavat*) refers to that which has undergone the "destruction" (*vaiśasa*) of the compound;
and this [refers to the document] in the reading "given to the Brahmins" (*vipradattam*).
Regarding the phrase *pitāmahapitāmataya*: "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) refers to Brahmā; he is the grandfather, the progenitor, of whom [the individual] is a descendant.
Of those two, birth and death;
[it refers to] one who possesses them, i.e., one characterized by birth and death.
"By those two, [namely] birth and death.
And it should be stated that "beyond which," [referring to] kings [extending] as far as the ocean.

Since the limit (*avadhi*) follows the same grammatical principle as the ablative (*apādāna*), it is understood here as ending in the fifth case (ablative); thus the justification for the counter-example is established.
In the phrase "upāgatam ete," the action of approaching is indicated by the word "upāgatāḥ. Regarding the term "raṇabhūṣitaḥ," it should have been stated as "raṇabhuvi" (on the battlefield).
The action consists in the state of being pitiable;
in this context, the prayer for reunion is presented as its cause.
Its status as a related factor—by way of its connection through that [action]—is expressed by the qualifier "Kapālin" (the Wielder of the Skull).
In this context, the word *saṃbandhin* (relational) functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvavṛtti*), denoting the state of being related (*saṃbandhitva*),
just as in the rule "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one," or in the expression "he spoke very firmly."
"That of hers" means that it is her qualification; [it refers] to "her," namely,
the prayer for union.
In that context, "having become objects of lamentation" refers to the state of being pitiable.
"Capability" means the power of accomplishment without deviation.
The word "tasya" (of him) is used in the sense of "sakala" (entire), and it refers back to the term "kapālinaḥ" (of the skull-bearer).
By the phrase "with the request for union with the principal object," it is indicated that [the subordinate element] is secondary in quality;
thus, "in this way, toward my father."
It should be understood that these qualifiers— namely "of the Noble One," "of Skanda," and "of you"— convey excellence.
"Of him alone" refers to Hara, who is the cause of the difficulty of being approached due to his majesty.
"That" refers to preeminence.
"Of him" refers to Hara.

"Of the imagined object" (*kalpitārthasya*) means because there is a superimposition of meaning characterized by mere stringency (*adhijyatva*) upon that which expresses merely an expanded artificiality.
"Of the unapplied" (*aprayuktasya*) means, according to the stated method, of that which is not employed by poets in this sense.
"The acquisition of another quality" (*guṇāntaralābha*) is due to the avoidance of the fault of not expressing what ought to be expressed, as will be defined later.
The word *mātra* [indicates] the instrument (karaṇa) in the sense of "it was done in this manner.
A *niṣka* is a particular kind of ornament.
The phrase "following a case-ending" (*vibhaktyanvaya*) means "of a case-ending that is actually heard [in the expression]."

And thus, by the rule "in the case of an insult, the genitive [is used]," there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that metaphorical representation (*rūpaka*) is accepted as instruction. When it is established— by means of another authority— that the world,

the Veda, and likewise the inner self (*adhyātma*) constitute the threefold authority in the manner already described, then the meaning is that one understands the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) through the implication of those things which bring about the excellence or deficiency of its own qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
The meaning is real.
He states the absence of elision (*aluk*) by means of the rule "in the sense of abuse, after a word ending in the genitive case.
It should be considered thus.
The meaning is that this must be investigated for the sake of understanding.

And as for the phrase "because of the elision of the case-ending in a compound," here indeed, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the presence or absence of the hearing of a case-ending serves as the actual causal factor for the two qualifiers.
However, when these [two] are encountered as occurring within a compound, they produce a lack of clarity regarding the predicate (vidheya) because the case-ending of the compound is not heard.
For this very reason, even in a compound, if a case-ending is heard, there is no lack of clarity regarding the predicate, as in examples such as *dāsyāḥ kāmukaḥ* ("one who lusts after a slave girl").
In that context, however, compounds were formed for the purpose of creating a single word-form (*ekapadya*) and so forth. The phrase "based on that" means based on excellence or deficiency.

And thus, it is demonstrated by pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the failure to discern the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the non-hearing of case-endings.
Having thus defined the *tatpuruṣa* compound in its sevenfold variety, he defines the *avyayībhāva*: "The *avyayībhāva*.

The construction is as follows: that which is the qualifier of "beloved" (*dayita*) with respect to the qualified object "nearness" (*samīpa*) is [the same] qualifier of "that nearness" (*tasya samīpasya*).
In the expression "in the midst of the sky" (*madhyevyoma*), there is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule "with *pāre* or *madhye*, or with a word in the genitive case."
The word *ca* (and) indicates excellence.
Thus, by this much, the operation of compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*)—with the exception of the *dvandva*—has been examined.
