Now, the operation of primary and secondary suffixes (*kṛt-taddhitavṛtti*) is investigated by means of extended application (*atideśa*), beginning with the words "by this very [rule]," and so forth.
The phrase “due to a specific intention to express” (*vivakṣāviśeṣāt*) involves the elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., *vi-vakṣā-vi-śeṣāt*).
The term *sarvakaṣaḥ*—meaning “that which scrapes everything”—falls under the scope of the suffix *khac* according to the rule *sarvakūlābhrakarīreṣu kaṣaḥ*.

Furthermore, this is the domain of the word *kukṣimbhariḥ*, which is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term meaning “one who fills his belly,” derived from the sense “he who bears [his belly]” (*bibhartti yaḥ*).

*Vidhnut* is derived from *vidhvaruṣos tud* [Pāṇini 3.2.35], which is the locus for the suffix *khaś*. *Śīrṣacchedam* is a word formed with the secondary suffix *yat*, according to *śīrṣacchedād yañ ca* [Pāṇini 5.1.65]. *Tais* refers to [actions] such as scratching (*kaṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of all objects," this refers to the womb as a characteristic of the body;

and regarding the phrase "and of the moon," it is clearly established that the intention here is to express preeminence primarily among those things that possess excellence; this is how it should be construed in its entirety.
And regarding the phrase "even of the severing of the head," it should be connected with the statement that there is an intention to express predominance while bestowing excellence.
Its separate mention from the preceding [qualities] is because it belongs to a different category by virtue of being the object of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formation.

And here, in the bestowing of excellence upon the four qualities beginning with "all things" (*sarvārtha*), the four [qualities] beginning with "granting fearlessness to the world" (*bhuvanābhaya*) mentioned immediately prior should be understood as the causes, respectively.
"That too" refers to his conduct.
"Among those who cause suffering and so forth" means among the wicked, the gluttonous, and Rāhu.
"I am Rāma; I endure everything."
The domain of the suffix *khac* [as in *dāśaratha*] is governed by the rule *pūḥsarvayor dārisahoḥ*.

For when it is said, "this is the progeny (*prasūti*) of Daśaratha," and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *ṭhak* (which becomes *iñ*) is applied according to the rule *tasyāpatyam*, this is the scope of the word *dāśarathi*.

However, regarding the sentence, although it was stated that "even if [it is a sentence]," it has been said: "A sentence is held to be that which has action as its primary element, possesses qualifiers (*guṇa*), and consists of a single meaning."
"Other" refers to the statement regarding the capacity produced by words (*śabdakṛtasāmarthya*), according to the principle that will be stated later.

"That" refers to the primary status (*pradhānabhāva*) previously mentioned in the phrase "by way of being the principal. This primary status belongs to all three—namely, those produced by the word, the meaning, and the intention to speak. "Produced by the word" means accomplished through the power of the refinement of the word (*śabdasaṃskāra*), as for example, the case of the final member of a *karmadhāraya* compound.

That which is produced by the force of the meaning and accomplished through the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*) is, for example, [the predominance] of the *graha* (cup) and so forth in such expressions as "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*).
Because it is that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*), it possesses predominance in reality.

That which is produced by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣākṛta*)—that is, established by the whim of the user—is that which is intended for the purpose of bestowing excellence or deficiency upon another; for example, [the predominance] of Rāma and so forth in such expressions as "Rāma’s hand is a sword" (*rāmasya pāṇir asi*).
Among those three primary elements, primacy belongs solely to that which is intended by the speaker (*vivakṣākṛta*),
for it is that which produces the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of the poetic meaning.
For this very reason, it has been said that there can be no "equality of status" (*samaśīrṣikā*) between them.
"Of those two"—that is, of those produced by the power of the word and its meaning—[the phrase] "together with that which is produced by the speaker's intention" is implied by the sense.
Now, was it not previously stated that primacy belongs to the verbal [meaning] only when intended by the speaker, while for the other [meaning], it is real?
How then is it said here that there is a difference between the verbal and the intended?

Alternatively, if there were a difference [between the two], what distinction would there be between the intention (*vivakṣā*) and the expressive power (*kṣati*) produced by the capacity of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), given that both establish the three types of predominance?
For it is said that the predominance produced by the capacity of the meaning is something other than that produced by the word itself;
thus, because that which is produced by intention has already been stated.
In that case, does it remain as something produced by the power of the meaning?
This is not a fault;
for previously, because it was the exclusive domain of grammarians and was produced by the intention of the grammarians, it was considered merely intentional (vaivakṣikatva).

For anything else that falls within the domain of a poet, its reality is precisely what constitutes its "objectivity" (arthatva). Here, however, for that which is the exclusive domain of the sensitive reader (sahṛdaya), its status as a "conceptual object" (vaivakṣikatva) is asserted by virtue of the poet's intention.

And for that which is the sole province of grammarians, its status as a "verbal object" (śābdatva) is established; thus, due to this difference in perspective, there is no contradiction with the former [definition].

Regarding the distinction stated between that produced by the capacity of the object (*arthasāmarthyakṛta*) and that produced by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣākṛta*) in the presentation of the three types of predominance (*prādhānya*), this is the underlying meaning: here, predominance is indeed twofold—verbal (*śābda*) and real (*vāstava*).

And since the reality [of predominance] does not depend upon intention, it is stated that its being produced by the capacity of the object is necessitated by the power of the thing itself (*vastusāmarthya*).

Even though there is a difference from what is produced by words, when the presentation of excellence or deficiency is prompted by the poet’s intention, that which is produced by intention is nonetheless established as being real.

And thus, by providing the Vedic example "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), which functions through the power of the meaning independently of intended expression (*vivakṣā*), the distinction between the respective domains is established; therefore, even the second contradiction does not exist, and everything is consistent.

Having thus deliberated upon the transferred (*ātideśika*) relationship of subordinate and principal in the domain of *kṛt* and *taddhita* formations, he now connects the subject at hand—the directly taught (*aupadeśika*) relationship—as it pertains to compounds, with the words "this very thing is here."
Because the rule *sarūpāṇām* (of those having the same form) follows the same logic as the *dvandva* compound, the formation of an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is also accepted.
The phrase "even in the absence of the relation of qualifier and qualified" clarifies the purpose of including the term *prāyaḥ* (generally) in the section on compounds. [The example is:
*rūpaṃ ca kāntiś ca vidagdhatā ca* ("beauty, grace, and cleverness").
The two examples—"by nectar" and "by poison"—are given according to the distinction between expressed and unexpressed agents.
For in cases such as *rūpam* (the form), the agency of the form and so forth is dependent upon the action of "becoming" (*bhavana*) which is understood [as implied].
By this, that which was stated in the context of providing examples of the agent for the *tatpuruṣa* compound—namely, "of the many case-factors, such as the agent and so forth"—[is explained].
That is what was intended. As for the phrase "who and who," the elision of one member (ekaśeṣa) has not been applied here;
rather, it is an instance where the elision has been applied, as in the usage "kāu" (meaning "which two").
Now he shows the attainment of the state of being primary and secondary with the words "yatra punar" (where, however).
The construction is as follows: "bhavataḥ" (of you two) is in relation to the wives of the enemies, and "ripustrīṇām" (of the wives of the enemies) is in relation to the pair of breasts.
"Of the wives of enemies" (*ripustrīṇām*) is an example of a compound (*samāsa*). And here, nothing more than a mere relationship is perceived.

"For that very purpose" means that figures of speech such as simile (*upamā*), poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), and so forth, are employed to establish either the excellence or the deficiency of the simile, poetic fancy, and the rest.
Otherwise, its composition would be purposeless.
"Those two" refers to excellence and deficiency.
By the word "compound" (samāsa), the intention that it is indeed a compound is being referred to.
Although, according to Vāmana’s opinion, the Pāñcālī style is free of compounds while the Vaidarbhī style possesses a moderate number of compounds; yet—
Nevertheless, since the opposite view prevails in other systems of thought, the Vaidarbha style is described here as being without compounds (asamāsā) with that intention in mind.
An example of a compound is given precisely within the middle of the verse, where the mere connection [of words] is perceived:
*ūrdhvākṣitāpa*.
In this case, when three quarters of the verse—lacking the single remaining element of the fourth quarter—are compounded, only the mere relationship is perceived, not the excellence or deficiency.
However, from the sentence (vākya), both are understood; the meaning is that the entity consists of both the form of the relationship and the forms of excellence and deficiency.
An example here is [the form] *me 'rayaḥ*; for if it were a compound, it would have to be *madrayaḥ*, and from that, no sense of superiority (*atiśaya*) is perceived.
Now, one might object: "But was it not stated that for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* following a word, the substitutes *te* and *me* occur in place of the singular forms?"
Nor is the word "asmad" (we/us) followed by another word here.
If it is argued that the word "eva" is the [following] word, we say no;
for its use is prohibited by the rule "na ca vā hā ha eva yukte," and because it belongs to a different sentence.

For the elision (nighāta), the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and so forth, occur only within a single sentence (*samānavākya*). By this very [principle], any separate word distinct from that is refuted.
Here, some say that the substitution of words is merely an elevation (*utkarṣamātra*), and that in a sentence, the apprehension of aesthetic flavor (*rasapratīti*) is fully established.
If, while providing incomparable delight through poetry, there should be even an incorrect word, it would not then be considered a gross defect;
for in poetry, the apprehension of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is paramount.
If that is not accomplished, there would be no poetry at all.
In the case of employing an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), however, it is merely a failure to remember the grammatical rule. As it has been said:

"A composition that is devoid of aesthetic flavor is a great *apaśabda* for a poet; because of it, he would be no poet at all, whereas another [who uses a correct word] might be one who simply forgot the rule."
Thus [it is said]. Others, however, say:

"Granted that an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) may have only a slight fault in consideration of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), nevertheless, the employment of an incorrect word by great poets is a grave defect."

Therefore, in this context, the words *teme* are included among the *nipātas*; thus, the word *me* is a *nipāta* that functions as a substitute for a case-ending, just as the word *aham* is used in expressions such as *ahantā* and *ahaṃyuḥ*.
Consequently, there is no distinction here whatsoever.
Is the instrument defective in its entirety?
No; he says "but rather" (kin tu) to indicate that this refers to the compound.
The word "in between" (*antareṇa*) refers to the fact that [rasas] such as the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*) are manifested through [the *vṛtta* and *vṛtti*].
The *vṛtta* includes the *vasantatilakā* and others;
the *vṛtti* includes the *kaiśikī* and others, as well as the *upanāgarikā* and others.

*Kāku* is either a modification of sound characterized by a change in tone (*kāku-adhyāya*) or it is the *vācika-abhinaya* (vocal expression), which is a modification of speech; it is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion). The phrase "having the half-verse as its limit" means that, with respect to the verse, the limit is the middle of the verse.
"Deficiency" (nyūna) means that, in comparison with the verse as a whole, the capacity to manifest rasa is deficient;
for example, in the previously cited passage beginning with "ūrdhvākṣitāpa" and so forth.
By the rule that "the compound should be made up to the end of the half-verse and not exceed it," this is an illustration of the excess that is thereby excluded.
The meaning of "of that" (*tasya*) is as follows: if the mutual relationship between the word-meanings is not severed, then no interruption should be made in the middle of that compound.
[The reason given is] "because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārāt*); for being the object to be predicated (*vidheyatva*) is indeed inseparable from predominance (*prādhānya*).
[The example is] "oil" (*sneham*).
In this case, since the drinking and so forth, as well as the illumination, are characterized by being enjoined, restated, or omitted, and share a single agent, there is no lack of predominance.

Furthermore, it has been established previously that it is defective to begin the reference to the lamp— the meaning of the word— by means of the relative pronoun *yaḥ* in the phrase "yo 'yam," and then to refer to the sentence-meaning by means of the demonstrative pronoun *tat* in the phrase "tattamasaḥ."
*Śakti* means power, capability, and a type of weapon;

It is like a peacock, whose crest is fire;
it possesses a shining, radiant luster belonging to the moon and gold;
and it has a shimmering, flashing radiance from its dark-blue eyes.

"In *andhakāre tamasi andhakāreḥ harasya*, *guhaḥ* refers to Kumāra. Regarding the phrase *apara iva*, because of the force of the word *apara* (another), there arises the cognition of the king being a second Guha; since that is impossible in reality, this constitutes a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the imagining of that possibility."
However, in the absence of another word [denoting the standard of comparison], this would be a simile (*upamā*) regarding the perception of the real Guha himself, abiding in his own essential nature.
The same should be understood in cases such as "like another Indra" (*apara iva pākaśāsanaḥ*) or "a second bowstring" (*maurvīm dvitīyām*).
Regarding the term *aharpateḥ*:
by the rule *ahar-ādīnām paty-ādiṣu*, the substitution of *repha* (the letter *r*) occurs.
Here, the qualities such as *dhāraṇa* (retention) and so forth are subordinate (*guṇabhāva*).
But the locus (ādhāra) possesses primacy;
for the agent, while accomplishing subordinate actions, accomplishes the primary action with ultimate intent, but does not have ultimate intent toward those subordinate actions themselves.
Where there is a primary purport (aidamparya) in all [the words], there indeed all [of them] possess the status of being denotable by the verb;
as in the example beginning with "from the palace" (saudhāt).
Anything else is subordinate.
The first [type] is primary;
the other is non-primary. The mention of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) is a qualifier for the rule "frequently with the qualified" (*viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*).
"Somewhere," and so forth.
Because the purpose of employing the term *bahulam* (in various ways) is established as "occurrence in some cases and non-occurrence in others":

the rule for compound formation (*samāsavidhi*) is the *utsarga* (general rule) because it is of a general nature; and its prohibition, being of a specific nature and motivated by the intention to express predominance and so forth, is the *apavāda* (exception).
"Of the exception alone" means that,
according to the principle that a general rule (utsarga) operates by excluding the domain of its exception (apavāda),
[the action] is impossible to perform.
Because its scope is not fixed;
for example, in the case of the general rule *utsargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam*,
this [restriction] does not apply when the word *pari* is present.
Regarding the term *parivāda* as *parīvāda*:

it does not occur in the case of *vivāda*. The intention is that there would be no compound because the mention of "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* lacks the necessary force (*sāmarthya*) regarding the relationship between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restatement (*anuvāda*), which is the context here. Thus, there is no compound.
"Tadabhiprāyam" means the intention of the teacher;
"sāpekṣatām" refers to [the case of] "the king's man," where the king is wealthy, and so forth.
That is the mention of "capacity" (samartha).

Regarding the phrase "the exclusion of this," the word "this" refers to the relationship between the primary and the non-primary. The meaning of "the mention of capacity" is that it serves also to exclude the application [of the rule] to cases where the primary and non-primary relationship is not intended here.
Regarding the term "the subject to be enjoined" (*vidheya-uddeśya*): here, the "subject" (*uddeśya*) is that which is to be restated (*anuvādya*), because it is fit for being indicated subsequently.
As for the phrase "by which [it is] so" (*yat tena*):
the word *yat* is connected to the preceding matter.
"Because of that non-completion," or "there is no designation," for it is stated that "kṛt, taddhita, and samāsa suffixes have the characteristic of being designators.
And there is the mention of the term "samartha" (semantically connected) with the word "or."
The word "ca" (and) here is redundant, because conjunction (*samuccaya*) and option (*vikalpa*) are mutually exclusive. And thus:

[If it were so,] his gaze would not be raining nectar, his face would not be dripping with the honey of a smile, his heart would not be moist with tenderness, nor would his limbs be like the touch of sandalwood paste.
In this regard, the two words *ca* and *vā* have been refuted,
because the meanings of *ca* and *vā* are mutually contradictory in a single instance.
As for the term *khaṇḍika*, it refers to a fragment related to the text, but not the entire text.
"It belongs to those who possess it.

Regarding the mention of "those by whom his intention has not been understood," for the Teacher, his intention had indeed not been grasped by them. [The phrase] "the depositing and extracting of the expression" [is used].
The "placing" (*ādhāna*) of designations refers to the introduction of new words;
the "extraction" (*uddhāra*) refers to the removal of those that were previously established.
"Shālīnas" means those who are timid, lacking in boldness, and devoid of critical inquiry.
"Aparam api" refers to repetitions and so forth. "Taccintā" refers to the consideration of whether there is a compound or no compound, depending on whether [the element] is primary or otherwise.

Regarding the term *prakaraṇa*: where, by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, the expressed meaning of a word reveals another meaning such as excellence or deficiency, in that case a compound must not be formed, for fear of destroying the intended meaning.
As in the case of "Rāma’s hand is a sword.
When the reading is "accompanied by context, word, and so forth," it is accepted that there is the proximity of another word.
When the reading is "accompanied by context, intonation (kāku), and so forth," [the meaning follows accordingly].
Then, by the term "intonation" (*kāku*), a specific modulation of voice is meant— such as tempo, articulation, pitch, and so forth— which is accepted as being present in poetry.

Thus, through a sequence of related and further-related topics, having elaborated at great length upon the intended relationship of subordinate and principal elements— as it pertains to compounds, as it pertains to their extension, and as it pertains to the operation of the whole— the [distinction] is now established with respect to the genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound in the example under discussion.
To provide the connection, he says, "It is situated thus," linking it with "the appropriation of Ambikā.
If one asks, "What is that? [it follows].
The function of the qualifier is either the exclusion of other lions or the communication of excellence residing in the lion.
In the first case, there is the possibility of the indicated aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).

The intended meaning, however, is that in the second [interpretation] a compound would be untenable. Furthermore, the word *vivakṣita* (intended) should be construed with the word *camatkārātiśaya* (excess of aesthetic wonder).
The phrase *tasyāḥ* means "from her," that is, from Ambikā.
A different genus (*jātyantara*) is a specific sub-genus of lions; that which is delimited by it is "distinguished. That which is distinguished alone is "supramundane" (*lokottara*).
"May Hari's bird Garuḍa destroy delusion"—
the meaning is "may he destroy delusion, which is ignorance.
[The phrase] "delimited by the class Garuḍa" [is used].
The meaning is that, according to the Buddhist view (*saugata-dṛśā*), there is a multiplicity of *garuḍas*;
however, their status as a specific class of birds is due to their distinctness from other genera and so forth.
This is the expression of his own intention.
The meaning is that this is by way of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on similarity.
By the word "her" (*tasyāḥ*), Sarasvatī is referred to;
the sense is that Ambikā is the reflection of Sarasvatī, and [the lion] is his own [reflection].
Regarding the phrase "in the second alternative":
this refers to the alternative of demonstrating the excellence residing in the lion (*kesarin*).
The meaning is that from the compound *ambikākesari*, that very aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) emerges.
Regarding the phrase "rise and setting":
in the commentary, the connection follows the sequence of the *cūlikā*, such that there is a "setting" of the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) and a "rise" in the sentence.
This has already been demonstrated previously by means of presenting examples and counter-examples.
Regarding the phrase "for what is desired": the non-attainment of that which is intended is what ought to be urged, [in the form] "this desired thing is not established";
however, the non-attainment of that which is not intended is an ornament.
The meaning is that this is not a refutation.
"By us" refers to this very aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
That [wonder] is indeed an error (*bhrānti*); and error is twofold, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and conceptual (*savikalpa*).
Among these, the first consists of the cognition of two moons and so forth by one whose sense faculties are impaired by cataracts and the like;
the second, however, is of the nature of conceit, consisting of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like.
"That" refers to the realization of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
"From the explanatory sentence alone" means from the sentence that analyzes the compound, namely, "the lion of Ambikā.
"Of them" refers to those who do not accept the diversity of cognition.
"Superimposed there" means that in that compound—which stands in the place of mother-of-pearl—the [meaning] is unreal, superimposed like silver [upon mother-of-pearl].
The two sides of rising and setting are respectively conveyed by the sentence and the compound;

[the author] employs the word "udyoga" (exertion) instead of the word "saṃrambha" (impetuosity) so that the sequence of words remains undisturbed, as if one were already engaged in what is about to be undertaken.
The word *adaḥ* (that) in the phrase "yo 'sāv" (he who is that) refers to what is well-known, because it will be referred back by means of the pronoun *tat* (that).
As for the term "pratipāditā" (established):
indeed, the sequence of introduction and conclusion based solely on the use of the pronoun *tat* has already been established as the underlying meaning.
Regarding the phrase "by means of a pretext" (*chaleṇa*): when the word *iva* is employed along with *chala*, this is a concealing poetic fancy (*sāpahnava-utprekṣā*).
Even when the word *chala* alone is employed, it is concealment (*apahnuti*).
When the word *iva* alone is employed, there is poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) upon the perception of a possibility;
but when both [the word *iva* and the particle *api*] are employed, the perception is variegated.
Furthermore, there is no commingling (*saṅkara*) of concealment (*apahnuti*) and poetic fancy here.
For poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is invariably concomitant with concealment (*apahnuti*);
that concealment is sometimes internalized, as in the example "as if nail-marks on the forest grounds," where [the word] "not palāśa flowers" is implied.
However, I consider that there is the apprehension [of the object] as "scratches from fingernails.
In some cases, however, it is expressed by means of a word, as in "as if he had ascended.
And thus, this [apprehension], being inseparable from concealment (*apahnuti*), functions as a sublater of concealment.
There is no confusion with that [other type],
for it occurs only when there is a difference in the sentences;
for in that case, the relationship between injunction and restatement is perceived directly and in its proper sequence.
The word "or" (*vā*) is a qualifier;
and that [qualifier] is to be enjoined when there is an intention to express the relationship between an injunction and a restatement (*vidhi-anuvāda-bhāva*).
[The phrase] "elsewhere" (*anyatra*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]

In the absence of being subject to increase, decrease, or injunction, there is "acting according to one's own will" (*kāmacāra*) in both the compound and non-compound forms. The phrase "for that purpose" means for the purpose of prohibiting the compound in cases involving increase and so forth.
The term "sāpekṣā" (dependent) is used solely for the purpose of conveying the principle that "that which is dependent is incapable [of forming a compound].

Just as in the expression "the parents are to be saluted," by the rule of constant connection (*nityasaṃbandha*), one understands "one's own parents" alone; likewise, by the rule known as "non-denotation of dependent elements" (*anabhidhāna*), the absence of compounding for dependent words is understood.
"Svatā" means "one's own," as if it were one's own property;
it refers to the cessation of various types of faults.
Now, in order to manifest his own excellence, he speaks the verse beginning with "kāvyakāñcana" (the gold of poetry), presenting his own labor in a condensed form.

Since it is poetry alone that must be examined—like gold—it is the touchstone itself that considers its own self to be the locus of examination; however, the touchstone is not the ultimate reality in the manner previously described.
For this very reason, there is even a derisive remark concerning the one known as Kuntaka.
"This verse" refers to that which has been demonstrated as the very essence of all; against it, such a shower of refutations has been unleashed.
By this, it is indicated: "What need is there to count other texts?"
This has been demonstrated by way of illustration, cited according to the maxim of "the grain in the cooking pot.

In this verse, following the logic that will be explained later regarding this very point, the word *kāñcana* (gold) is marred by the fault of tautology, because gold is already implied by the term *kaṣa* (touchstone), which denotes a fixed rule. Furthermore, some discerning scholars maintain that in the phrase *nijakāvyalakṣmaṇi*, the formation of a compound is vitiated by a lack of consideration for the predicate (*vidheya*), since the meaning of *nija* (one's own) serves as the locus of emphasis and thus ought to be the predicate.
The author himself has already provided the answer in his own works by stating, "unrestricted by [rules of] truth" (*tattvenaiva granthakṛtā svakṛtiṣv ayantritaḥ*), and so forth.

Furthermore, since this failure to discern what is to be enjoined (*vidheyāvimarśa*) falls under a vast number of well-known examples, we have demonstrated its detailed analysis in various places in our *Nāṭakamīmāṃsā* and *Sāhityamīmāṃsā*; therefore, for fear of making the work too prolix, we shall desist right here.

Having thus characterized the failure to deliberate upon what ought to be done through its various forms, he says, "There is also a breach of the sequence of presentation" (*prakramabheda*), in order to characterize that breach.
In the phrase "of the cognizer's comprehension" (*pratipattṛpratīteḥ*), the comprehension of the cognizer occupies the position of the chariot.
An "excavation" (*utkhāta*) is a place that is unevenly elevated.

"Enam" refers to the linguistic usage of words and their meanings. "Being its object" means being the subject matter of a different context. "Not addressing" means the absence of speech performed by that [person].
In this way, non-addressing is to be understood.
"Inadequate" means incapable.
It is because of the acceptance of the mode of being [as] a statement of injunction or a restatement; here, "mode" (prakāra) means similarity.
For that which has been introduced stands as the subject (anuvāda),
and that which carries it forward appears as the predicate (vidheya).
In this regard, he provides a clear example of the manner of the predicate and the subject, beginning with "yathā" (as follows).
Virtues arise only when they are perceived by those with sensitive hearts;
lotuses become truly lotuses only when graced by the rays of the sun.
In this very way, people attribute the likeness of the moon's orb to her cheek;
yet, when analyzed from the perspective of ultimate reality, the moon is merely a wretched moon.
This is merely a matter of elevation and depreciation; there is an intention to express the elevation of the lotuses, whereas for the moon, there is an intention to express its depreciation.
For this very reason, two examples have been provided.
Regarding the phrase "the manner of breaking the sequence" (*prakramabheda*), here "manner" (*prakāra*) refers to a specific distinction.
As for the phrase "breaking the sequence of synonyms" (*paryāyaprakrama*):
it is not appropriate to indicate the meaning of the word *candra* by means of another synonym, *śaśin*, because that would entail the aforementioned fault of breaking the sequence.
"And not thus" means that there is a conclusion by means of that very same word.
"Of those two" refers to the deviation from the initial course and the tautology.
"Of this" is a reference to the non-deviation from the initial course.

For in that case, there is no redundancy between the brief statement (*uddeśa*) and the detailed explanation (*pratinirdeśa*), because the flow of understanding proceeds with a single, uniform character.
The relationship between that which is briefly stated and that which is explained in detail is not a domain of redundancy; for example:

"With limbs emaciated, with faces washed by falling tears, they tread upon the ground strewn with *darbha* grass, their delicate fingers wounded and dripping blood as if their feet were stained with falling lac.
Here, two instances of the word "falling" (*galat*) are specified; it is logical that this constitutes a case for "correspondence according to the order of mention" (*yathoddeśa-pratinirdeśa*).
[The phrase "of those two" refers to the lack of uniformity in the sequence of introduction and the tautology.]
The word "iti" refers to the non-deviation from the initial course [of expression]. Now, one might object: in the example "O father, where are you going?
(*vrajan* *kva tāta vrajasi*), since there is a departure with the root *vraj-* and a conclusion with the same root *vraj-*, how is there no deviation from the initial course?
Anticipating the objection that *vaja* is also a verbal root—since it is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as *vaja vraja gatau* (to go)—it is stated: "of one who goes.
The word *uditam* (spoken) is an adjective qualifying *śiśunā* (by the child), and its purpose is to indicate that the meaning has been fully understood.

And [the word] "asphuṭam" (unclearly) here functions as an abstract noun. For one traveling on a road for the sake of some business, it is improper to call out a name from behind; thus, when his name was uttered by a child with playful words, his mother rebuked him, and because of that, he felt resentment.
The intended meaning here is "increased.

Having thus demonstrated the deviation from the established sequence (*prakramabheda*) regarding that [nature] which consists of verbal roots (*dhātu*), he now demonstrates it with respect to its form as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), showing the variety of its types through pronouns and so forth,
by means of the words "sarvanāma" and so on.

Furthermore, in some manuscripts, after the illustration of the deviation from the sequence of the base (*prakṛti*), an illustration of the deviation from the sequence of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is seen, followed by the instruction on the deviation from the sequence of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
In that context, it is appropriate to instruct on the suffix immediately after the base; thus, that [suffix] alone was mentioned, which constitutes the logical connection.
Following that, the deviation from their respective sequences regarding specific bases, specific suffixes, and their combinations will be examined.
"By the aforementioned method" means:

by the sequence stated in the passage "he who is mentioned as the agent in a single sentence, and he who [is mentioned] by 'this' and so forth. Now, one might object: "How can there be a conclusion with the word 'that' (tacchabda) when the opening was made with the word 'which' (yacchabda), or with 'this' and so forth, or even with the word 'which'? To this, he says: "And it is not thus."
Regarding the phrase "mutually dependent":
it has been stated that there is a constant syntactic connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.

In this same way, it should be understood that when words such as *idam* (this) and so forth—which denote objects not remote from the referent of *tat*—occur, as in the previously mentioned passage beginning with "that which is without conceptual construction" (*yo 'vikalpam*), the same principle applies.
"By this" (*tena*) is the conclusion of the subject under discussion.
Although there is mutual internal variety among these [causes] beginning with "this," they have a single purpose when viewed from a gross perspective.

Regarding the phrase "for here" (*atra hi*): for here, by means of the qualification of the agent, one [cause] functions as a cause indirectly while the other functions directly; thus, there is a difference in the method of exposition (*prakramabheda*).
Regarding the phrase "in order to attain fame" (*yaśo'dhigantum*), there is indeed a disparity in the cognition produced by the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and the suffix *-tumun*.
As for the word *vā*, he will state later: "where the word-meanings are of equal status."
"The reading *apatyavato 'pi* is appropriate.

On this point, some offer the following justification: "It is observed that people feel affection particularly for their own sons; therefore, even though the word *putra* denotes a specific kind of offspring while the word *apatya* denotes offspring in general, because of the influence of the pronoun [in the compound], the meaning necessarily resolves upon the specific [son]."
Regarding the phrase "the fulfillment of the primary subject matter":
this was said without having perceived the intention of this author,
because two distinct sentence-meanings have been composed here in the form of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and its corresponding subject (*dārṣṭāntika*).
And in that regard, it is appropriate to explain two things by way of the relationship between an original object and its reflection;
furthermore, in this illustration, there is a general introduction followed by a specific conclusion.
Because the word "flower" (puṣpa) denotes a general category while the word "mango" (cūta) denotes a specific instance,
and because a specific instance is an object of non-satiety precisely due to its excellence;
in the case of the illustrative example, the introduction of a specific instance is undesirable.
This is a general summary:
either, by the force of the word "all," it is logical to indicate another specific instance;
or, in the established reading, the word *putra* (son) expresses a particular, while the word *apatya* (offspring), which expresses a general category, culminates in that particular.
But when the reading is *yadā tv apatyavato ’pi*, then this constitutes a general introduction followed by a specific conclusion;

for the second occurrence of the word *apatya* reaches its specific application through its connection with the pronoun (*tat*), just as in the opinion of certain [teachers] regarding the phrase "some clouds on that mountain.
If the semantic coherence of the word *api* is observed, it indeed shines forth clearly.

Let there be no lack of satisfaction for one who has no connection with offspring regarding a single daughter; however, it is a matter of wonder how one who possesses many offspring can feel such affection for only one. It is precisely for this reason that the word "api" (even/also) remains significant. Furthermore, the cause of dissatisfaction regarding the daughter lies in her being destined for transfer to another.
And she is a vessel of affection due to the weight of her virtues;
for this reason, there is a comparison of hers with the *cūta* tree.
Therefore, the reading "even though he has offspring" (*apatyavato ’pi*) is indeed superior.

The phrase "the impossibility of compounding" means that there is an acquisition of another quality according to the maxim "it is better [to have something] than its loss," rather than a total abandonment of it.
"One for whom virtues are destroyed" (kṛtaguṇa) means one whose virtues, having been cultivated or acquired, have been ruined or lost.
A "non-jewel" (*amaṇi*) is an ornament that lacks a jewel;
here, by the word *upala*, a jewel itself is intended.
Since the word "jewel" (*maṇi*) is not employed here [in its place], there is a violation of the uniformity of synonymous terms (*paryāya-prakrama-bheda*).
"Like the sky," etc.:
the correct reading is "the swan is like the moon, and the moon is like the swan. This refers to Arjuna, the son of Maghavan (Indra).
And regarding the phrase "among the wise," it is intended as a reason that both "energy" and "the perception [of energy]" are present;
whether they are to be understood as a conjunction or an alternative.
The phrase "the conceptualization [arises] in order to attain fame" is cited here as an example of *vikalpa* (disjunction);
however, the phrase "this is the vigor of the conjunction" (*samuccaya*) is the example for *samuccaya*.
In the reading "vigor [resides] in the wise son," knowledge is not intended to be expressed as the cause.
Rather, he considers that [the statement] is intended solely to establish the true nature of the thing;
and thus, he has not reflected on how the qualification "among the learned" would otherwise result in being rendered meaningless.
As for the phrase "the state of being from a base family":

When there is an initial presentation using grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) followed by a subsequent reference using non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), it results in a breach of the established structure (*prakramabheda*). In this case, within the fourth quarter [of the verse], in the phrase "the skull itself is the glory of the stainless crest" (*kapālam evāmalaśekharaśrīḥ*): first, while the plurality of skulls ought to be expressed, the singular expression is used; second, while the substratum (*dharmin*) consisting merely of the "crest" ought to be stated, the expression "the glory of the crest" (*śekharaśrīḥ*) states a quality (*dharma*) instead. This is [an instance of that fault].
It must indeed be understood as untenable.

Thus, although an investigation is possible regarding the examples mentioned previously and those yet to be mentioned, it has not been carried out exhaustively here for fear of excessive prolixity; therefore, one should apply oneself to that very subject.
This is what is meant by "endowed with that."

Since it will be demonstrated that a designation by means of its own word or by a pronoun yields an equal result, Dharmakīrti’s usage in the *Vārttika*— "O Mother, look [at me] through your grace toward the Blessed One"— is thereby refuted by this principle.

It has been stated, "due to the absence of predominance," in reference to the case where there is a single agent performing multiple actions that possess both primary and secondary status; as in the example *anenijuḥ*,
meaning "they washed."
*Jakṣuḥ* means they ate;
*bisaprasūnam* means a lotus.

Regarding the phrase "in cases such as *nejanāt*," although the suffix *liṭ* introduces the category of the remote past (*bhūtānadyatana-parokṣa*), the resolution is made through the simple past (*bhūtānadyatana*) in the form *aneñjir*.

Likewise, in the case of *dhṛtavikāsī*, where the suffix *kta* is applied to a mere past participle (*bhūtamātra*), there is also a breach of the sequence of time. In that [previous] instance, the second type—a breach of the sequence of finite verbs (*tiṅanta*)—did not occur;
thus, here, by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the example *dhṛtavikāsī* is understood.

Regarding the phrase *anenijuḥ*, no resolution has been made here by taking it to mean "they placed his flower in full bloom," because it will be supported in another manner later on by the words "yadi vā" and so forth; [the author] thereby refutes this deviation from the established style (*prakramabheda*).

Regarding the word *ajayat* ("he conquered"), although the victory was not witnessed (*parokṣa*), it was not intended to be expressed as such because it was worthy of being seen; therefore, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) was not employed.
He provides an example for the case where something that exists is not intended to be expressed: "the girl has no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*).
For indeed, there is no absolute absence of a belly in any girl; rather, because it is slender, even that [existence] is not intended to be expressed. And so:
"The son of Diti, possessing the brilliance of the sun, became a groundless one through fear of the birth of his adversaries."
"Regarding the passage beginning with: 'That which they call the unprecedented golden couch of Hari, which destroys the very meaning of the word "Indra"...
[Rāvaṇa says: "Dear one, if you have been sent to heaven by your own splendor alone, may it be well with you; but do not speak before my friend the story that 'the bride was carried off by another.
If I am Rāma, the descendant of Raghu, then let the victorious Rāvaṇa himself, along with his kinsmen, speak while his neck is bowed with shame for all that."
Thus, there is nothing defective in this great stream of poetry.
Regarding the phrase "of the object" (*arthasya*): its being that [object] is "objecthood" (*arthatva*), which is existence; its not being that is "non-objecthood," which is non-existence.
The word "wherein" (*yatra*) is the remainder of the first half-verse.
The word "yathā" (as) connects with the phrase "there is no deviation from the sequence. In that context, a specific time is indicated.
Just as the distinction between present and non-present time, and between perceptible and imperceptible, is merely a matter of intention (*vaivakṣika*),

so too are those meanings such as *śīla* and the rest specified in the rule "from the root *kvip*, in the senses of one who has that habit (*tacchīla*), that duty (*taddharma*), or who performs it well (*tatsādhukārī*).
And their existence or non-existence is likewise merely a matter of intention.

Thus, even when suffixes such as those denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*) are employed in one instance, their non-employment elsewhere is not defective. For example: "Fearless, he protected himself; unafflicted, he practiced dharma;
free from greed, he acquired wealth; and unattached, he experienced happiness."

Thus, in this context, although the suffix denoting habituality (*tācchīlya*) and so forth is employed in the word *agṛdhnur*, there is no fault even if one does not employ [the suffix] in *atrasta* or *atrasnu*; or, if the term *atrasnu* is used, *agṛdhnur* is likewise entirely without defect. The state of having the fruit belong to the agent is what constitutes "intentionality directed toward the agent" (*kartrabhiprāyatva*).
That too is merely a matter of intention.
And thus, in the case of the verse, "She casts her gaze downward when seen, and remains silent when addressed," if the fruit of the action were intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāyatva*),
then the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in "she gives" (*dadāti*) would be untenable.

If it were not so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *parasmaipada* ending in the phrase "na cet tadā kuruta" (if you do not do so then); thus, the objection regarding a break in the initial grammatical structure (*prakramabheda*) has no basis whatsoever.
This should be understood in other instances as well.
Therefore, [the reading is] "tena te."
The meaning is that those specific times and so forth have not been shown by him for the reason that they were prompted by his intention to speak.
Regarding the word "gāhantām" (let them plunge):

here, the introduction of the agent through the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) while leaving the object unexpressed was intended; however, by using "visrabdhaiḥ" (with confidence), it was done otherwise, which constitutes a breach of consistency regarding the grammatical factors (*kāraka-prakrama-bheda*).
The meaning is that *vihṛti* refers to sporting (*viharaṇa*), that is, being the recipient of various graceful modes (*bhaṅgi*).

In the reading *vivṛta*, the meaning is the state of being expansive (*vistaraśālitva*). Regarding the conflict (*vigraha*) or opposition (*virodha*) in love: because it is separated by the breasts, it is impossible for that opposition to be carried out due to their intervention.
The suffix [in *vitene*] denotes the abstract state (*bhāve pratyayaḥ*).
The meaning is that the thunders became expanded (*stanitāni vitatībhūtāni*). This is called a "verbal" (*śābda*) breach of uniformity because it pertains to the word itself.

Regarding the objection that this is a "deviation from the verbal sequence" (*śābdaprakramabheda*), those who recite the subsequent text as both verbal and semantic in sequence have failed to consider the meaning; therefore, this [objection] should be disregarded.
As for the term *saṅgamabhūṣā*:
here, in a bahuvrīhi compound, the sequence is concluded by means of a meaning in which the referent of the other members (*anyapadārtha*) is subordinate.
Because its object is the word "bhidyamāna" (being split), this is a verbal *prakramabheda* (deviation from the established usage).

Similarly, regarding the phrase "thus [is] an objective (*ārtha*) *prakramabheda*," it should be explained that it is called "objective" because its object is the meaning "being split" (*bhidyamāna*) which was first introduced.
The term *dhṛtavikāsī* was previously cited under the section on time (*kāla*).
This is now illustrated as an instance of verbal scope (*śābdaviṣayatva*);
it may also be inferred from its occurrence within a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*).
For this is not a "discrepancy of sequence" (*prakramabheda*) based on meaning (*ārtha*); thus, two examples have been provided here: *mattatā* and *samatayā*.

In this context, regarding the word *mattatā* (intoxication), the sequence [of the root] is established by its underlying meaning (*ārtha*) as "adorned with passion" (*saṅgama-bhūṣā*), whereas in the word *bhūṣayati* (adorns), there is a reference back [to that same sense] through its literal form (*śābda*). Thus, there is a breach of the uniformity of the underlying meaning (*ārtha-prakrama-bheda*). However, the reading *tadvapus tad api cārutaratvam* is not logical, as it lacks conformity with the established order of the sequence.
The reading "cārutā sa khalu sāpi śarīram" is indeed superior; and in this case, the word "eṣā" (this) should be read as "dayitasaṅgatir eṣā," rather than the reading "āsām."
In that context, by which word is "intoxication" (mattatā) referred to?
This [word] "by equality" (samatayā) is generally seen as an example of a breach in the verbal sequence (śābdaprakramabheda) in various commentaries;
or rather, is it in the discussion concerning a breach in the semantic sequence (ārthaprakramabheda)?
And regarding the two examples just cited, the reading "āhitaviparyayam" for the first one is incorrect;
this is because it contradicts the text of the *Yojanā* commentary, which states, "the sequence of the meaning of Varuṇa.
However, even though the reading "niyamayan" was offered by Vidagdhamanyatā, it is not pleasing to our hearts.
There is no evidence for the claim that this [term] is connected with Varuṇa alone;
for Varuṇa, being situated as a subordinate to another, possesses no independence,
and such a connection does not bestow upon him the quality of abundance.
In the discussion concerning the breach of the sequence of meaning (*arthaprakramabheda*), this very example is superior with the reading *āhitaviparyayam*.
[The phrase] "the two are avoided" (*parihṛtau bhavataḥ*) uses the dual number because both the breach of the sequence of case-endings (*vibhaktiprakramabheda*) and the particle *ca* are twofold.
Furthermore, the particle *ca* is faulty in both ways;
moreover, the scope of the particle *ca* is conjunction (*samuccaya*),
and its absence has already been stated.
Since the deviation from the established context (*prakramabheda*) has already been refuted by the statement that there is no equality of status [between the two alternatives],
it should not be combined with the [objection] regarding the proximity of usage;
for that [deviation] ought to be recited immediately after the words "because of the restriction" (*niyamanāt*).
The "movement of clods" (*loṣṭasaṃcāra*) is a specific method of calculation consisting of the manner of joining each individual division with the other divisions.
Regarding the phrase "of the base and the suffix," the light word is the base (*prakṛti*);
within that, there is a division by means of the heavy word.
Furthermore, in the word *guru*,

the suffix *īyasun* is employed where it was not employed in the word *laghu*; and since no corresponding indication of that suffix is made [in the former], there is also a break in the continuity of the grammatical operation (*pratyaya-prakrama-bheda*).
In the new recension (*abhinavapāṭha*), however, the term *laghu* is used as a reference specifically for that which lacks the suffix *-t*.

Since the sequence of enumeration (*uddeśakrama*) that was commenced is not maintained in the subsequent reference (*anudeśa*) due to this inversion, there is a loss of perceived identity; thus, it is considered defective.
Regarding the phrase "your state of having flower-arrows":
this example of a deviation in the sequence of presentation is not appropriate, as it is precisely the sequence of the *cūlikā* (supplementary section) that is fitting here.
For such is the formal statement (*uddeśa*).

Setting aside the direct address toward Smara, it would be more appropriate to have a non-literal cognition directed toward the moon as a contextual subject; therefore, the initial mention of Smara is justified.
However, in the case of the subsequent mention, it does not seem fitting for the completion of the sentence-meaning to occur through a contextual element while abandoning this primary subject;
rather, the sentence-meaning must be brought to completion by Smara himself, who is made the focal point at the conclusion. Thus, with respect to the order of recitation:

This very *Cūlikākrama* (the sequence of the crest) is that which delights the hearts of the connoisseurs; this should be carefully examined by those whose intellects are as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass.

Accordingly, the usage seen in the *Cūlikākrama* is as follows: "In place of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when they stand in the sixth, fourth, or second case after a word [ending in a case-suffix], *vām* and *nau* [are substituted].

Furthermore, an example illustrating the distinction between *krama-prakrama* (sequence-break) will be examined in the section discussing the analysis of *vastu-prakrama-bheda* (distinction in the sequence of subject matter).
Because a word is employed to convey the meaning of that which is primary, and because the word is merely a means (*upāya*), and because there is no fixed rule for means; as it has been said:
"Those things which, though being adopted, are to be abandoned, are called 'means';
and no fixed rule for means is necessarily established."
Thus: "the violation of the established order" (*prakramabheda*).

Since the object of the violation of the established order consists in the manner of being either a prescription (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), the meaning is that the violation of the established order is also, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), a type of prescription or restatement.

By this very logic, one should understand that the violation of the established order has two divisions—verbal (*śābda*) and semantic (*ārtha*)—because its objects are words and meanings respectively.
Regarding the phrase "difference of words":
this is stated so that the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the object may be established through its being denoted by the non-difference of a single word.

For if there were a difference of words, that very same object would be perceived as if it were something else, and thus it could not, in a direct manner, be the subject of the relationship between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restatement (*anuvāda*).
For it is with reference to poetry that this reflection has been introduced.
And in poetry, unlike in scientific treatises (śāstra) and the like, words are not employed merely for the sake of conveying a meaning;
rather, it is the word and its meaning together that are employed therein.
"Sāhitya" (literary unity) means being on an equal footing, neither deficient nor excessive.
The sense is this: "Let it be so" is a general acceptance of the deviation from the established order (prakramabheda), whereas the objection applies specifically to particular cases.
The reading "pratītihṛdayaṅgamaḥ" (pleasing to the heart regarding the rule of deviation from the established order) is the one that touches the core.
In the expression "by means of whose difference and non-difference," the pronoun *yat* refers back to the initial subject (*prakrama*).

However, in the reading where there is a perceived restriction regarding the shift in the initial subject, the reference to the very initial subject as it was introduced—namely, "by means of whose difference and non-difference"—must be explained in some way or another.
[The phrase] "it purifies and adorns" [is used].

In this context, what was introduced as "ornament" (*bhūṣaṇa*) in the verbal form of "it ornaments" (*bhūṣayati*) is here referred to by its functional form as "decoration" (*alaṅkriyā*) and so forth.

Furthermore, although the deviation from the introduction of synonyms (*paryāya-prakrama-bheda*) exists here, it has not been considered at present, because the current occasion is the consideration of deviations regarding the sequence of words and meanings (*śabdārtha-prakrama-bheda*).
In this regard, [the phrase] "of the division itself" (*vibhāgasyaiva*) is used.

In this context, the word "or" (*vā*) implies that the object of comparison (*upameya*) is connected [to the quality] by way of its meaning, whereas the connection is not made explicit by the words themselves. "By way of the opposite" means due to the absence of a direct verbal connection.
In the two examples, the qualities are "it purifies" (*śuci bhūṣayati*) and "beauty adorns the body" (*cārutā vapuḥ*).
The meaning is that, according to the intention of the established reading "yādṛśam," there is impropriety, whereas according to the intention of the emended reading, there is propriety.
By the word "tat" (that), others are referred to.
[This refers to] "only similarity."
In that case, the word *tat* would have to be neuter.
Therefore, it is understood that [the word] "surāri" (enemy of the gods) is what is being referred to here, because of the lack of discrimination and the inability of his intellect to discern.
Thus, by the phrase "stolen by her," the variety of the figurative expression (*bhaṅgibhaṇiti*) is what is intended.

The meaning is that the object of description is concealed by an intense variety of expression (*bhaṇiti*). As it was said by the author of the *Vakrokti*: "Just as worldly ornaments are taken as models, so too [poetic] ornaments, appearing through their own nature, [conceal the literal meaning]."
The object of adornment, which resides within its own excellence of beauty, is thereby manifested.
Thus [it is said]: "There would be a lack of primacy.

This is the intended meaning: if the established position were that what is the object of the word's operation possesses primacy, while what is the object of the meaning's operation lacks primacy, then it would follow as a consequence that the threefold *pratīyamāna*—which others have designated as *dhvani* and which we have demonstrated to be inferable (*anumeya*)—would lack primacy, because it is the object of the meaning's operation.
Since the status of being the object of the word’s operation has been refuted,
yet primacy is nevertheless accepted,
how then can this perception of primacy and non-primacy be accounted for?

Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with *cakrābhighāta* and others, it was established previously that in the figure of speech known as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), the suggested meaning alone possesses primacy, not the expressed meaning, just as in the case of *samāsokti*.
As for the reading *ekābhighāta* in the *Hayagrīvavadha*, it is the established version, because *yaḥ* refers back to *sudarśana*, which is masculine and has been introduced [in the context].
If that [word *tat*] were to refer back to the discus (*cakra*) without understanding its intended meaning,
then the pronoun *yat* would take a neuter gender;
therefore, with the intention that Murāri alone is what is being referred to here, they read the text as "cakrābhighāta" (the blow of the discus).

But this is not the context there. It is with reference to that [context] alone that there is primacy and non-primacy. Here, the means (*upāya*) is subordinate because it is the instrument of comprehension (*gamaka*), while the goal (*upeya*) is primary because it is the object of comprehension (*gamya*).
Because that which is being perceived is what is understood (*gamya*), it is designated as "primary" (*prādhānya*);
this is not in consideration of the act of perception itself.
This refers to the cognition [produced] by both the word and its meaning.

The meaning is that, with respect to that [other], there is no conventional designation of primary or non-primary status. However, in this context, the investigation has been conducted by way of objects that are distinct from the relationship of the signifier and the signified;
and it is precisely with respect to that [distinction] that [the statement] "and with respect to that" is said.

Even for that which is denoted (vācya), there is the application of the designation "primary" by virtue of its being verbal; yet even for that, in relation to the other—that is, in relation to the status of the signified and the signifier—there is non-primacy in certain cases, namely where the suggested meaning (pratīyamāna) is present. This is the sense.

The intended meaning is that the expressed (vācya) is established as the indicator (*gamaka*) with respect to the suggested (*pratīyamāna*); therefore, because it is dependent upon that [suggested], it lacks primacy.
"Expressed through various artistic turns" refers, for example, to the works of Bhaṭṭabāṇa in their respective places. "[Because of being overwhelmed]"—and so forth.
As stated by the author of the *Dhvani*:
"The defect caused by lack of proficiency is concealed by the poet’s power.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and because of the difference in sentences": since the variety of stylistic expression (*bhaṅgibhaṇiti*) in one sentence is indeed relative to another sentence, it does not manifest the defect of a break in the initial course (*prakramabheda*), because there is no deficiency in the cognition [of the intended meaning] in that respect.
"Because it is established by logic (*nyāya*). Here, "logic" refers to the disparity between the verbal expressions.
The phrase "even of a difference in causes" implies that not only is a difference in cognition the cause of differentiation; [it is also the case for a difference in causes].
This applies even to the difference in causes.

The distinction between cognition is the cause of difference with respect to representation (*vijñapti*), whereas the difference in causes is [the cause of difference] with respect to production; this is the distinction. Thus it has been said:
This very thing is the difference between entities, or the cause of their difference: namely, the attribution of contradictory properties and the difference in causes.
Here, the variety or lack of variety in the manner of expression is the cause for the failure or non-failure of comprehension;
and "that" refers to the aforementioned difference in the sequence of presentation.

The verbal and the non-verbal (arthika) varieties of the breach of uniformity (*prakramabheda*)—which were previously characterized and illustrated as distinct from the specific types such as that of the root-stem (*prakṛti*) and so forth—have now been stated in general terms as the verbal and non-verbal breaches of uniformity that pervade all varieties of breach. This distinction should be understood in terms of their final resolution (*paryavasāna*) with respect to the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the implied meaning (*pratīyamāna-artha*).
This concludes the section on the "breach of uniformity regarding the subject matter" (*vastu-prakrama-bheda*).
*Vastuprakramabheda* (deviation from the intended subject matter) occurs when there is a failure to carry out the description of a subject exactly as it was begun to be described;
"by way of deviation" (*bhedena*) means by way of connection with its parts.
For in the first quarter [of the verse], the description of the whole (*avayavin*) itself in its own form was commenced; therefore, carrying it out by way of connection with its parts is a fault.
"In both cases" means in the description of the whole and in the description of the parts.
"That nature" refers to the nature of the heroine.
"O limb" is a form of address.

"Let it fall" means let it go downward. Regarding the phrase "in order to establish similarity," in the reading *dvicandram* (a double moon), the moon brings about a state of double-moonhood for the sky together with the face;

and since that is rooted in the similarity between the face and the moon, there is a breach of the initial course (*prakramabheda*) because similarity is introduced while the context was one of contrast (*vyatireka*).

Regarding the phrase *vastusargapaunaruktyasya* (of the repetition of the creation of objects), in the commentary on the verse *punaruktavastuvirasaḥ*, the interpretation was made that "he is tasteless (*virasa*) because of repeated objects," thereby resolving the difficulty through similarity (*sādṛśya*). However, since this contradicts the initial syntactical structure (*prakrama*), it remains a flaw. Some others, however, have supported the reading exactly as it stands by resolving the difficulty through contrast (*vyatireka*), interpreting it as: "He is tasteless regarding repeated objects" (*punaruktavastuṣu virasaḥ*), meaning he does not create repeated objects.
"Of the faults of meaning" means of those consisting in the transgression of the formal sequence;
"by heat [comes] the rains" means that by heat the rains [occur], and by autumn the arrival of winter.
And as Śiśira met with the splendor of Vasanta, all the seasons,
performing the task of bringing forth blossoms, assumed the status of resident householders in that city.

For here, while the description of the seasons is undertaken in the form of three pairs of women and men, the seasons in their female forms are intended to be subordinate due to their connection with the third [member of each pair]. Yet, in the case of "tapena varṣāḥ" (the rains by heat), an inversion has been made;
or, even if such a designation were made, there is a further alteration in cases such as "śaradā himāgamaḥ" (the arrival of winter by autumn).
This is indeed a case of "deviation from the sequence" (*prakramabheda*).
At most, we recognize this as a deviation regarding the sequence because the order in which the woman and man are introduced here has been handled otherwise.
Therefore, this very example should have been given previously under the category of "deviation regarding the sequence."
Therefore, the reading should be "tena varaṃ ghanaśriyoṣṇaḥ śaradā himāgamaḥ" (Better that there be heat from the beauty of the clouds than the arrival of winter through autumn).
There is also a break in the sequence of the agent (*kartṛprakramabheda*).

This occurs where agency residing in the referents of the second and first person pronouns (*yuṣmadasmadartha*) is intentionally superimposed by the speaker upon a remaining entity, whether sentient or insentient.
The meaning is that in this case, the superimposition of another agent for the sake of aesthetic charm is indeed a merit (guṇa), namely the transposition (vyatyāsa).
"Of those two" refers to where there is a deviation from the established procedure regarding the agent and the transposition.
"It is not determined by the context.

For, in this case, the agency of the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* has not been introduced as something to be expressed by the word itself, even though it may be determined by the context and so forth; thus, this is not a case of the fault of "deviation from the intended course" (*prakramabheda*).
This was stated by superimposing [the agency] elsewhere, namely upon Rāmabhadra, who is intended to be the subordinate element (*śeṣatvena vivakṣite*).
In the same way, the distinction [of otherness] should be applied later to Bhārgava and Vaṭu as well.

Now, one might object: since the referents of "you" and "I" are sentient, it would be more appropriate for the insentient alone to be distinct in relation to them; so how can it be that only the sentient is distinct? To this he says: "For it is of two kinds.
This is the intended meaning:
The distinctness of another entity does not depend on its being conscious with respect to the referents of "you" and "I," but rather depends precisely on its being the referent of "you" and "I.

And these two referents of "you" and "I" consist, respectively, in the state of being other (parabhāva) residing in the object being addressed, which is called "I-ness" (asmitā), and in selfhood (pratyaktā).
Consequently, in relation to that [specific instance], the remainder is "other.
And since that [remainder] is twofold—consisting of the sentient and the insentient—there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Furthermore, with the sequence "by the axe" and "Candrahāsa," there is an example of the transposition of agency regarding insentient objects for both the referents of *yusmad* and *asmad*.
"O Lord of Laṅkā!"—

here, since Rāma himself is the one making the request, another example of the transposition of the agenthood denoted by "we" (asmad-artha) onto an insentient object, though it exists elsewhere, has not been considered for citation because it was already considered in a previous instance.
And because of the introduction of another topic of reflection:

thus, having examined the "deviation from the sequence" (*prakramabheda*) by means of this much of the treatise, he says, "The deviation from the sequence is as follows," in order to examine the "deviation from the order" (*kramabheda*), which has now arrived in its turn.
Now, if it is asserted that the referent of the word *tat* (that), which functions as a recollection and a reference, has only an object that has been previously experienced, [then...]

Regarding those such as Rāma who are absolutely beyond the senses, how can they be referred to by the poet in his poem using their own names, given that they are supersensible? To this he says: "And here, there is merely a cognition.
This is the intended meaning:
that without which something else cannot be established.
Its dependence on that [perception] is logical.
Furthermore, since memory is untenable without mere cognition (*pratīti*), it must depend on that;
it does not depend on sensory perception, because we observe that such memory is possible even without sensory perception, as it occurs through words and other means.
And if Rāma and others were not perceived through the senses, then let their cognition arise from verbal testimony or from common renown;
and since their reference is made by the word "that" (tat), which functions as a reflective pronoun based on that [cognition], there is no contradiction whatsoever.
[The opponent asks: "But surely..."?
This is the meaning here:

since the investigation of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the investigation of the meanings of its constituent words, let this doubt arise during the time of investigating the word-meanings.

However, at the time of investigating the sentence-meaning, because there is no appearance of a temporal sequence of prior and posterior within the undivided cognition (*akhaṇḍapratīti*), there is no room for this defect.

And since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is internal because it is the intended object (*uddeśya*), when the systematic arrangement is established by relying on that [cognition] alone, there is no consideration whatsoever of the fault of sequence.
"Corresponding" means having the nature of a reflection; "its movement" is the transmission of the speaker’s intention.
This refers to "the linguistic usage of words."

The meaning is as follows: by way of linguistic usage (*śabdavyavahāra*), the reflection on the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthavimarśa*) grasped by the listener is accepted [as being] that of the speaker. If linguistic usage—which culminates in the listener’s reflection—were not of a nature that is a counterpart (*praticchandaka*) to the speaker’s reflection, then, because the reflections of the speaker would have no connection with the words, there could be no inference.

And in that regard, the phrase "and this [perception]" means that within the deliberation on the meaning of the sentence occurring in the minds of both speaker and listener, there certainly exists a manifestation of sequence, though it is subtle and thus not clearly manifest. The phrase "in the cognition of word-meanings" refers to that which precedes the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
The phrase "even there" [is used] for this reason.

The meaning is that even when examining the meaning of a sentence as it resides in the speaker and the listener, a subtle fault based on the word-meanings is difficult to avoid, because the examination of the sentence-meaning is established precisely by means of transcending the individual word-meanings; thus, [the fault] is said to be "born of negligence.
This being so, the fault of failing to reflect upon the matter about to be undertaken is thereby included.
"Because of the cause for going against [the current]" refers to "because of the construction of a bridge by elephants";
it is "verbal" because it ends in the ablative case.
"By the mention of its bathing-place" means that there is an intervention by the word "its bathing-place" (*tadīyatīrtha*) between the cause and the effect.
"By way of the qualification of the Gaṅgā" refers to the reading "gajasetubandhām.

The intention here is this: where the relationship of cause and effect is expressed directly through words (*śābda*), there should be no intervention between the two by means of stating the cause, because that would result in a remoteness of comprehension (*pratītiviprakarṣa*).

In the case of the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), because the reason (*hetu*) presented as a qualifier has already fulfilled its purpose by describing the nature of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is no remoteness of cognition despite the intervention [of other words],
since the cognition of its causal status arises through the power of reflection (*paryālocana*).

And here, although the two words "tīrthe" and "tadīye" could have been omitted since the meaning of the sentence remains complete even without them, their inclusion is indeed superfluous (apuṣṭārtha).
By the word "tadā" [is meant] by the pronoun "tat";
thus, the word "tat" refers to the cessation of superimposition (*āropa*). Here, "superimposition" (*āropa*) means error (*bhrama*), which is the cognition of one thing as being another.
Just as in the case of a fresh rain-cloud being described as having the proud appearance of an armed night-stalker,

when that [superimposition] is to be negated— as will be explained here— it is proper to refer to the real object of superimposition, such as the cloud, which is manifesting, by means of a demonstrative pronoun like "this" (idam); and in that case, it ought to be employed in close proximity to the thing being referred to.
However, an application that places something unreal in proximity to what is being superimposed brings about a disruption in the sequence.
But as for this first application, which is in proximity to lightning precisely by way of the nature of the object of superimposition itself, there is no room for any other objection.
Like a mountain whose peak has been uprooted, like a lotus pond struck by frost and abandoned by its beauty,
like a goblet drained of wine, or like the night of the full moon bereft of the lovely moon.

Regarding "itīva": here, the meaning of the preceding sentence, which consists of the act of perceiving (*upalambha*), is imagined as being delimited by the word *iti*; therefore, the words *iti* and *iva* should be employed before the word *upālabdha*. However, because they are used in relation to a different object, there is a change in their sequence [from the previous construction].
This is done by means of the word *prāpipayiṣu*, which remains as part of the meaning established in the preceding sentence.
"Dependent on that" means being subject to the person.
"Stambaram" is a term of praise used because of the sight of her two full and elevated breasts.
"Ṣidgāḥ" refers to libertines.
The "diversity of cognition" refers to the comprehension or non-comprehension of the sentence-meaning when its elements have been reduced to a state like sesame and husks.
Regarding the "nature of the utterance":
the utterance is this very statement: "This elephant (*stamberama*), desiring to mate, approaches."

The true nature of that [word] connected with the *viṭ* (the base) is intended to be distinguished by means of the word "iti" and so forth, because [the former] serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, in that context, from that word "iti"—that is, from what is indicated by the word "iti"—and from the "evam" and so forth which were previously mentioned, namely, those shown before, no other word such as *ṣidga* and the like should be stated; this is the meaning.
The same should be applied to other examples as well.
Regarding the phrase "because of being a limiting adjunct" (*upādhibhāvāt*), the word *iti* has its own power, which consists in delimiting the preceding sentence;
by surrendering that [power] to the preceding sentence, the word *iti* becomes its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
And therefore, the meaning is that its application should not be made elsewhere;
"of another word" refers to [words] such as *ṣid-gaiḥ*.
"Otherwise," that is, when applied to a different domain, there would be incoherence, characterized by a fragmented or inconsistent understanding.
Regarding the rule of immediate succession (*ānantarya-niyama*):
whatever is connected with something else, it belongs to that [latter] even if it is situated at a distance;
for in the case of things that are not semantically related, mere proximity is no cause [for connection].
The meaning is that, by this principle, through the force of the propriety of the sense, there will be a rule of immediate succession even for those [words] that are separated.
"From elsewhere" means from the force of the propriety of the sense.
"Because of the accomplishment of that task," etc., means because of the accomplishment of what is to be done.
Thus it was said that their application would be restricted.
[An objection: "In which case should the logical connection of one thing with another be established? To this he says: "By some only."

The meaning is as follows: by excluding words such as *iti* and so forth, and by following the aforementioned sequence while avoiding other words such as *śabda*, *hetu*, and so on, this rule applies to those other words.
However, for words such as *iti* and the like, there is this specific domain of restricted usage;
they must not be employed otherwise.
Having thus reflected upon the variation in sequence according to the order of the headings, he says "repetition" (*paunaruktyam*) in order to examine the issue of redundancy.
Indeed, in this context, repetition is of two kinds: verbal repetition and semantic repetition.
As it was stated by the Sage Akṣapāda: "The restatement of word and meaning is a repetition, except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*)."

In this regard, there is no fault in the repetition of words provided there is no repetition of meaning; however, it is faulty when there is a repetition of meaning, because it is the meaning alone that is the determining factor.
The collective sense is that repetition of meaning alone constitutes true redundancy, not the repetition of words.
"Based on the object" (ārtham) means dependent upon the object;
the same should be stated for "based on words" (śābdam).
