"As has been said" refers to the *Vādanyāya*.
The word *hasati* occurs twice: one instance is the noun *hasati* ending in the suffix *śatṛ*, functioning as an adjective qualifying the master (*svāmin*);
the other is a finite verb. The same should be understood for the subsequent cases.
Regarding the term "yantra": it is a designation for a servant by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), because he imitates what has been done [by his master].

This is because there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparyabheda*) elsewhere; for when there is a difference in intended meaning, provided there is no distinction in the literal sense of the form itself, *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) is desired. Thus it has been said:
Indeed, when there is no difference in the meaning of the essential form, a repetition of words or phrases is intended as *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) for the sake of a different effect.
Thus: "O one resembling Śakra," "O swan of the glorious river," "O moon of the earth," and "O time of enemies"—these are the four vocatives.
Here, the difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*) is quite clear.
For instance, the single word *kāśa* is established as the object of comparison for garments.
But in the other case, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is distinct because the *hasa* (laughter) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Other instances should be construed in the same way.
"In the absence of both" means the absence of both a difference in meaning and a difference in intended meaning.
The meaning is that there is no difference in intention (tātparya) regarding whether "ghāsa" (grass/food) is connected as either the object (*karman*) or as a relational term;
this is what is negated by the phrase "na ca.
[This refers to the view] "svārtham" (for its own sake).
This is what is meant: the *tātparya* (intentional focus) is not merely the expression of its own primary meaning;
rather, it is the further orientation toward another meaning while the expression of its own primary meaning is indeed present, as in the case of the words "kāśa" and "śaya."

In that case, because a substance delimited by the genus *kāśa* is presented, a relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) distinct [from the substance itself] is conveyed.
This is not the case with the two words *bisam* and *bisinī*.
For here, no entity whatsoever is perceived apart from the substance delimited by the genus *bisa*.

As for the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and the status of being related (*saṃbandhitva*), these belong only to that which is already denoted; they do not bring about a state of otherness through an intensification [of the meaning]. Therefore, it is logical that these are the proper domain of reference by means of a pronoun, excluding the word itself.
Now, is this not a redundancy? It is said: where there is comprehension of the meaning without its employment, and where the employment of another word identical to it is necessarily required.
In that regard, how is there tautology?
Where there is comprehension through a single meaning and no difference in intended purport, there is tautology because it results in a sense of distaste for the comprehension.

However, as for that [word] which is identical to another word, let it be employed or not; in any case, the distaste caused by its employment is what constitutes tautology (paunaruktya). It is on the basis of this that the aforementioned fault is stated.

Regarding the term "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*): in the example *jakṣur bisam*, the lotus-stalk (*bisam*) mentioned previously is worthy of being referred to by a pronoun in its subsequent connection with the flower; yet, because it is expressed by its own specific word, [it is considered a fault].

That is a verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*). Although it was previously stated that there is only one type of tautology, namely semantic tautology (*arthapunarukta*), it is nevertheless described as a "tautology of the word" with the intention that the word's tautology occurs precisely through the medium of the meaning.
To distinguish the fitness (*yogyatā*) indicated by the phrase "of that which is capable of being referred to by a pronoun," he says: "predominance."
The fitness for being referred to is twofold: verbal and objective.
Among these, that in which the object of reference possesses primacy through an independent designation as the agent and so forth is verbal;
whereas, where the object of reference is designated as having some other relation [to another], [it is objective].
In that case, it is the purpose; for in that context, its fitness consists precisely in its utility with respect to the related entity.
And thus, one example has been cited.
"By way of the cognition of a related entity":
here, the related entity is Hara (Śiva), because [the moon] is related to him through his crown;
and it is by way of the cognition of that [related entity] that the moon is cognized here.
But in examples such as "beauty is the body," there is no direct perception of the moon itself, as there is of beauty and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of those related to the moon":
here, that which is intended as the "related thing" (saṃbandhī) in the verse is the connection (saṃbandha).
That has been indicated;
likewise, here the rays are indicated as being related [to it].
By the word "that" (tat), the moon is indicated as that which is capable of being referred to by that [word].
Regarding the phrase "for that [moon] is subordinate":
with respect to the referent of the other word, namely Hara, the lord of night (the moon) is subordinate;
and with respect to him as well, the night is subordinate.
And as for the phrase "she is Bhuvana," here the relationship belonging to the daughter of the Lord of Mountains is not indicated;
rather, by the words "she is," her essential nature is indicated.
"Vihasta" means incapable of anything.
The connection is with the word "parāmṛśyasya" (of that which is to be referred back) within the compound.

For in that case, since that which is to be referred back has become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) within the compound and its relatum (*saṃbandhin*) has not been specified, a reference back (*parāmarśa*) is not logical.
"Not to be perceived by all people"—

this is its meaning: according to the principle that "the universe revolves in whatever way it pleases him," the author, with great boldness, has begun here to establish a system of categories dependent upon his own [will],
by which he justifies— even though it would otherwise be untenable— the reference by the word *tat* to both the moon (*tadaṃśunicitaḥ*) and the night (*tat tamasām*).

And regarding the verse, "They ate the lotus-fiber, [the bees] whose lotus-blossoms were blooming in the clarified butter," one might raise the objection that there is the fault of tautology (*paunaruktya*) based on a subtle scrutiny of the word *bisaprasūna*, even though it is a proper name (*saṃjñāpada*), because it relies upon the word *bisa*.
However, this justification does not strike the heart,
for both *śaśāṅkamauli* and *niśāpatimauli* are likewise proper names.

Furthermore, although names and words possess a correspondence with their referents, this correspondence does not function as the primary determinant, because conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) holds predominance.
Consequently, in this context, there is neither the meaning of "hare-marked" (*śaśāṅka*) nor the meaning of "night" (*niśā*).
Rather, relying on these two meanings merely as expedients, it is specifically a particular named object (*saṃjñin*) that is intended here.

Thus, by referring back to those two—the moon and the night—which are included within the compound *saṃjñin*, this [use of the pronoun] wins over the hearts of sensitive readers; however, this is merely a forced justification. Furthermore, in the case of *śaśāṅkamauliḥ* ("the one with the moon on his crest"), it would be better for the moon (*śaśāṅka*) to be referred to by the pronoun, because its curved form is present there;

whereas in the case of *niśāpatimauliḥ* ("the one with the lord of the night on his crest"), the reference to the night (*niśā*) is more wretched than even the wretched, since the lord of the night (*niśāpati*) alone is present there according to the aforementioned sequence.
Since night serves merely as an illustration, it is impossible for it to exist there;
and where even that itself is impossible, what need is there to speak of darkness? Thus, this is like the blind man who found a jewel.
The maxim "he caused him to eat with his fingers removed" follows from this principle.

Furthermore, where a designation is communicated by means of a word that follows [the object] through its extension (*anugama*), there, due to the excellence of that extension, there occurs a reference by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*). For example:
May he who adorns the crescent moon, the beloved of Rohiṇī, be born for the festival of the world—
he whose body, though smeared with white ashes, shines as if filled with her own radiance.
Thus, in this case, the designation that extends over the entire quarter of the verse indeed enhances its propriety;
therefore, the reference here does not cause a lack of comprehension.
In the present instance, however, even such an interpretation is not possible.
Or let the subject at hand rest;

for even here, in examples such as "the lover of Rohiṇī" (rohiṇīramaṇa), if a subtle scrutiny is applied, then because the name is predominant, the reference to that portion by means of a pronoun does not incur fault.
In the present case, however, the reference is more sinful than sin itself.
The author has already provided a justification for this matter:
"This is merely his way of proclaiming the preeminence of himself, who considers this entire universe to be insignificant.

However, the intention of the author is as follows: "In this context, there are two kinds of technical terms (*saṃjñā-śabda*): conventional (*rūḍha*) and those based on both etymology and convention (*yoga-rūḍhi*)."

In that regard, one should not follow those words that are conventional (*rūḍha*), because they lack any connection to the [etymological] meaning. However, as for those that are both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*), if the etymological sense (*yoga*) is predominant, then usage based upon it is not faulty.

For this very reason, the Buddhists have strictly prohibited the use of a word that functions by the force of its primary cause (*nimitta*) when that cause is already included within another term. As they say:

The interpreters of scripture (naimittika), by conforming to the meaning of the Veda or to another ultimate meaning of words, have described how there is no contradiction [between scripture and reasoning].

Thus it stands. When linguistic usage is based on such a [derivative] yoga, if some non-deviant meaning that constitutes a component of a name (*saṃjñā*) is intended to be expressed, then the reference to that component by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) for the sake of connecting it [to the whole] is not faulty.
As it has been said: "Of that which is concealed by the function of a compound, [the connection is made] by means of a pronoun."

In the expression *mauli* (crown), rays—which are invariably concomitant with the moon—are presented as its attribute. In the expression *niśāpatimauli* (the crown of the lord of night), darknesses—which are invariably concomitant with the night—are intended.
Furthermore, the fact that these [attributes] are unreal does not constitute a fault in such cases.
This is because it has been established as being within the scope of poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
The only distinction is that in the former case, the object of reference is connected to the named thing (saṃjñin), whereas in the latter, it is connected to what is related to the named thing.

Thus, in this way, for derivative (yaugika) technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*), linguistic usage based on their etymological derivation (*yoga*) is indeed well-established in various instances. As for the objection that in the phrase "I might [do] even to Hara, the wielder of the Pināka," the term *pinākapāṇi*—being a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*)—will have its etymological meaning precluded, necessitating the word *hara* for the sake of understanding the name;
that is not intended to demonstrate an absence of etymological meaning.

However, the intention is that when an object being followed is intended as the locus of intense emphasis (*saṃrambha*), its expression cannot be accomplished without the employment of a distinct nominal term, because there can be no simultaneous predominance of both the referent of the name and the object being followed; thus, in such instances, the employment of both is indeed recommended.

In the present context, even though [the word] is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) for the purpose of conveying merely the essential nature of the thing, the pursuit of its conformity with the meaning remains unimpeded.
"Otherwise" means that in the absence of both kinds of fitness, there would be no cognition of the object to be referred to. "But here," however—
In the phrase "jakṣur bisam" (they ate the lotus stalk), [the word "bisam"] refers to the connection with the flower; that is, its acquisition.
This is based on the sense (*ārtha*).

Since the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is expressed by the verbal form (*ākhyātapada*), it is introduced here through the verbal sequence; however, because it is presented here by means of a compound (*samāsa*) as a qualifier, the meaning is considered "implied" (*ārthatva*). And since that [implied meaning] is of many kinds, the term "that" (*tat*) refers back to avoid redundancy (*paunaruktya*). In brief, five types of redundancy are indicated.
Regarding the form *aśvīyā*:

here, by the rule *keśāśvābhyāṃ yañchau*, the suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). Thus, both the suffix *cha* and the word *saṃhati* are mentioned again as the base forms (*prakṛti*) for the case ending *bhis*.
For indeed, one should simply say "with horses";
however, one should say "bisā" [meaning] "having provisions consisting of cuttings of lotus shoots," and "tvag-uttarāsaṅgām" [meaning] "having bark as an upper garment.
Regarding the term "bahuvrīhi," this is a prescription for forming a bahuvrīhi compound in the sense of possession (matvartha).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the *karmadhāraya* and the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*"):
the meaning is that the *karmadhāraya* and the possessive suffix, when present together, are superseded by the *bahuvrīhi* due to the parsimony of its application (*vṛttilāghava*).
Now, one might object—
The suffixes *matup* and others occur in the sense of abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, excellence, association, and when the existence [of a quality] is intended to be expressed.
Thus, many meanings such as "ground" (*bhūmi*) and so forth, which follow the sense of the verb "to exist" (*asti*), have been stated as being the domain of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*).

To the question, "Why have these not been stated as being denotable by the *bahuvrīhi* compound? he says: "of the *matup*. The mention of *matup* is an illustration for all possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*).
For meanings such as "abundance" (bhūman) and so forth are not understood from the possessive suffixes (matup, etc. alone;

rather, they are understood from those suffixes when assisted by context and other factors. Therefore, they are not cited in the investigation of the possessive suffixes, because they are already included therein by necessity.
In the expressions *jāmbavena*, *tadīyena*, and *vanyena*, there is a redundancy of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*). [Likewise] in *jambūpallavāni* and *tanmātaṅga*.

And in the case of *vanakariṇām*, since the meaning of two operations—the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and the determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*)—is understood through the genitive compound alone, there is no redundancy here.

In the word *vārtraghna*, what is intended is the descendant of Vṛtrahan (Indra); it does not mean "this is the slaying of Vṛtra," and thus there is no redundancy of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in this instance.
Regarding the phrase "samūhārthāyāḥ" (of that which has the sense of a collection): in the rule *grāma-jana-bandhu-sahāyebhyas tal*, the suffix *tal* is applied to express a collection (*samūha*).
Here, since the meaning of "collection" is already understood from the word *jana* itself, there is a redundancy between the base form of the suffix (*tal*)—which is plural—and the suffix itself.

As in the previous case, in expressions such as *dalatkandalā* ("with bursting kandalas"), *lambāmbuda* ("with hanging clouds"), and *phullāmbuja* ("with blooming lotuses"), there is the fault of tautology (*punaruktatva*) because the meaning [of the object] is already understood through the bahuvrīhi compound itself.
Regarding the phrase "only the substantive" (*viśeṣyamātra*): the cognition of the substantive occurs either as an unqualified substantive or as a qualified substantive.
Among these, in the case of cognition as a qualified substantive, it occurs where the substantive itself is cognized from the qualifiers alone.
In that case, the employment of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is not faulty, as will be explained later in the phrase "by his grace" (*tatra prasādāt*).
However, in this instance, the meaning of the word *bhava* is already understood through the mere mention of the means by the expression "ornamented with the cool-rayed moon" (*śītakiraṇābharaṇa*),
just as in the phrase "as if the earth were pregnant with a treasure" (*nidhānagarbhām iva sāgarāmbarām*), the meaning of the earth is understood through the word "ocean-clad" (*sāgarāmbarā*).

*Camūru* is a particular species of deer; *kutha* is a multicolored woolen rug. Regarding the phrase "of one or the other": when the word *indravāhana* (Indra’s vehicle) is employed, there is the cognition of the Lord of Elephants (*nāgendra*) due to the implication of the *kutha*; and when the word *nāgendra* is employed, there is the cognition of Indra’s vehicle because of the description of its white color.
Thus, the employment of only one [of the two terms] is logical.
By the passage beginning with "where *tat*," etc., he illustrates the comprehension of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) by way of its being a qualified form (*viśiṣṭa-viśeṣya-rūpatayā*).
"Its particularity" (*tad-viśeṣaḥ*) means the particularity residing in the qualified object.

The meaning is as follows: by the word *pinākapāṇi* (the one who holds the Pināka bow), a specific quality residing in Hara is expressed—one intended as the cause of his supreme excellence—and not merely the bearer of the name.

This occurs even without the explicit mention of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), for the word *kusumāyudha* (the one whose weapon is flowers) also conveys the substantive, as it is invariably associated with it.
But there is no separate application [of the suffix] for that [word *asmad*].

Regarding the phrase "here too," [it means] "only by the third person (*liṅ-uttama-puruṣa*) in the case of *pinākapāṇeḥ*. For, since the rule *asmady uttamaḥ* ("the third person occurs after *asmad*") includes the phrase *sthāniny api* ("even when [the word *asmad*] is not present"), the third person indeed occurs whenever the meaning of *asmad* is possible, even if the word *asmad* itself is not employed.
"Non-apprehension of that" means non-apprehension of the qualificand.
Regarding the phrase "of others":

the intention is that because the plural number is used, the meaning is already conveyed by a single particle *eva* in such contexts; therefore, the employment of other [particles] would be fruitless.
The meaning of the sentence "for the third as well" is as follows: when one intends to express a comparison between whole sentences (*vākyārtha*), only a single particle *iva* should be employed.

However, when one intends to express a comparison between individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), as many *iva* particles must be used as there are word-meanings functioning as the subjects of comparison. The point is that one should not apply the "half-old woman" principle (*ardhajaratīya*) here.

And this has been stated as a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*); however, his position is not that when a comparison of sentence-meanings (*vākyārthopamā*) is possible, comparisons of word-meanings (*padārthopamā*) should be employed.
Thus, he will refute this with the words "day after day" (*dine dine*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "day by day":
here, the crescent of the moon serves as the point of comparison for Pārvatī, while the various digits serve as the points of comparison for her specific qualities.

And the qualification "consisting of the beauty of the particularities" refers to those [moonbeams] which are like the various arts (*kalā*); for the explanation is: "those whose [beams] are among other moonlights."
In the verse beginning with "day by day" (*dine dine*), the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) belongs to both Pārvatī and the crescent moon.

However, the interpretation that "other digits" (*kalāntarāṇi*) are the agents who nourish "other rays of light" (*jyotsnāntarāṇi*) is not correct, because it would entail defects such as a discrepancy in the grammatical number of the words (*vacanabheda*). Furthermore, in this context, since the sense that "the lunar crescent nourishes other digits" is already conveyed by a single *iva* particle, the use of a second *iva* is redundant.
Regarding the phrase "having encountered whom":
here, "whom" (*yam*) has the fierce wind as its喻 (upamāna, point of comparison),
and the word "Cedi" (*cedi*) has a lamp as its point of comparison.
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "equality.
The abandonment of Śambhu’s grace occurs precisely because of the pacification of his eyes.

Furthermore, even if the reading were provided here, the fact that the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), being in the accusative case, are embedded within heterogeneous words such as *lalāṭalekhayā* (by the line of the forehead), makes the employment of distorted words unavoidable and results in a lack of aesthetic flavor (*vairasya*).
Thus, the reading "caṇḍamārutanavapradīpavat" (like a new lamp in a fierce wind) is superior. For,
by merely substituting the word "na" for the word "mi," there is a slight modification that allows for the easy comprehension of the avoidance of faults as well as aesthetic beauty.

The poet’s intention is that the phrase "as if moist with sandalwood paste" is presented as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the crescent moon, and by virtue of expectancy, proximity, and semantic fitness, it results in becoming an epithet for the surface of the forehead.
However, in reality, since the desired effect is achieved even without the use of the word *iva*, the word *iva* is redundant;
furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever in fancying the crescent moon to be moist with sandalwood paste.
And wherever this qualification is applicable, the use of the word *iva* is redundant;
for in a compound such as *tadabhinnārthena*, the sense of *iva* is already internalized.
"By way of reversal" means because it is suitable for application near the surface of the forehead.
Regarding "it is better," there is no lack of satisfaction because the displacement of the word *iva* has not been avoided.
Since the term *kevala-hārī* was not formed as a compound, the sense of *iva* is not perceived; thus, the word *iva* is not redundant, and the avoidance of tautology has been accomplished.

"Aho aparyanteti" (O, infinite!)— the term "od" is designated as a *pragṛhya* (non-sandhi) vowel; according to the rule beginning with "upamārūpaka," where there is one ornament within another ornament, it is called by the poets an *alaṅkāra*.

"Those who are not satisfied [with mere suggestion] bind [the meaning] with necklaces and the like, as if with a bracelet"—thus says the author of the *Vakroktijīvita*. However, he criticizes that ornament which falls into the category of "flowering ornaments" (*alaṅkārapuṣpa*). In the phrase "like the sloughing off of a snake's skin," the nature of this as both a simile (*upamā*) and a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is stated according to the consensus of others.
But this is not a simile-based metaphor (*upamārūpaka*); rather, it would be a metaphor based on poetic fancy (*utprekṣārūpaka*),
because the slough is perceived as being imagined (*saṃbhāvyamānatvena*).
For instance, first of all, the sky is figuratively represented as a snake because of its suitability for shedding its skin;
and once the metaphor has been fully established, the mention of the "shedding" is not perceived as a detached fact,
but rather as something belonging to the snake in the sky.
And when there is a cognition [of the cloud] as being connected with a serpent in the sky, it is not a matter of similarity (sādṛśya), but rather a case of identification (adhyavasāya);
and since that [identification] is what is currently operative, poetic fancy (utprekṣā) alone is superior in such a cognition.
For this reason, the expression "this" (iyam idam) was employed.

Otherwise, if one were to establish a pure similarity (*śuddhasādṛśya*), the subject (*dharmin*) itself—being distinguished as the "shedding" (*nirmoka*)—would have to be designated as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
If it is argued that it was not so designated because a comparison between two bases of different genders is defective, we say no;
for [the defect applies] even when the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not designated, or when, even if designated, it lacks the dual form, or when there is a difference in gender and number.

In such cases as "This eunuch moves like a woman," and "Just as faults strike down kings, so here virtue strikes down ill-behavior," the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is intended;
therefore, in a simile, it should be "like the sloughing off of a snake."

In *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), the fancying of an action alone is possible; therefore, this is in reality a *utprekṣārūpaka* (metaphor based on fancy). This has been explained by us in detail in the *Harṣacaritavārttika*, and should be understood from that very source.
The same should be stated regarding examples such as "like an axe" (*paraśur iva*).
Regarding the phrase "like the flame of the forest-fire of darkness" (*tamo-raṇyavahner ivārciḥ*):
here, fire (*vahni*) is intended to be connected with the flame (*arciḥ*) by way of its form as "darkness-forest" (*tamaso raṇyena rūpeṇa*), and it must be included within the compound;
for there is nothing specified here that could be qualified by "fire."
Therefore, one ought to say "the flame of fire for the Tamara forest"; in this case, the failure to state what should have been stated is a fault.
The example of the superimposition of the relationship between the object of attribution and the attributor occurs even when similarity exists, as in "it kisses, as it were."

In this case, since the word *iva*, employed for the purpose of a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*), has its function fulfilled by a meaning established through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is redundancy (*punaruktatva*).
Furthermore, regarding such passages where [the author] intends both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*), the author of the text has offered a critique based on mere pedantry (*hevākitā*).
Likewise, an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is a striking distinction (*vicchitti*) of either word or meaning.

Furthermore, because *vicchitti* (artistic grace) consists of the radiance of a poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and because that radiance is infinite, it partakes in infinity and cannot be fully delimited.
For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* stated:
"Even by thousands upon thousands of Vācaspati-s, with all their effort..."
Once bound, it does not go to destruction, just as the nature of the worlds [remains constant].
Thus it has been said elsewhere:
"Even now, O fisherman, the movement of your speech is not yet exhausted.
And in this way, if there were redundancy of one figure of speech in relation to another figure of speech, then there would likewise be redundancy of simile in relation to metaphor and the like.
For, in comparison with simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*) or hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is more powerful;
yet it is not employed in this manner, because the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*) varies.
For instance, in some cases mere similarity is intended;
even there, in some instances non-difference [is intended];
and in that case as well, in some instances superimposition [is intended].

In some cases there is determination (*adhyavasāya*); even within determination, there is sometimes the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatva*) and sometimes the state of being established (*siddhatva*). In this manner, there is an infinite variety of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-vicitrya*).

Furthermore, how can the ever-new variety of aesthetic charm—experienced and employed by great poets through the process of combination—be denied on the grounds that [the audience] has a taste for brevity?
For this statement is not a treatise on grammatical definition, whereby one would consider the brevity of syllables;
nor even in that case did the great ones invariably resort to brevity.
For indeed, in place of the term *vāgrahaṇa*, the term *anyatarasyām* has also been employed;
even by them, a variety of stylistic breaks (*vicchitti*) has certainly been adopted.
As it has been said: "The composition of Pāṇini’s Sūtras is indeed diverse."

Thus, even when a metaphor (*rūpaka*) has been employed here, the inclusion of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) or similar figure enhances some particular quality rather than being a defect; this should be carefully examined by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*). It should not, however, be attached as a mere affectation; let that matter rest for now.
Let us return to the subject at hand.
"Murmura" means charcoal.
In the phrase "of the mango grove," there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* due to the prefix *pra*.
[The term] "surrounding the throngs of travelers."
In the case of the construction with *paritas* joined with a word denoting sound, the accusative case is used after *abhitas*, *paritas*, *samayā*, and *nikaṣā*.
Here, the word *iva* in "as if they placed" (*dadhuḥ iva*) is indeed redundant;
for since the particles of dust, which are one thing, are perceived as having a very close similarity by being held to possess the nature of the powder of embers, which is another thing. Thus—
May that lotus from the navel of the Lord of Śrī protect you— the lotus which serves as the hall of Vedic study for the Lotus-seated One,
where the bees provide an imitation, as it were, of the sounds of the Sāman chants with their long humming.

In such instances as these, where an imitative word (*anukāra-śabda*) is employed, the use of words such as *iva* should be understood as redundant. Regarding the phrase "from the figure of speech *prativastūpamā*": since the similarity is already perceived through the *prativastūpamā* in the line "the great ocean longs for the rising of the full moon," the explicit mention of the word *dṛṣṭānta* (example) is defective.
Nor is the word *dṛṣṭānta* used here to establish the presence of the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta*.
Because the term *dṛṣṭānta* (example) does not convey the status of being a "figure of speech" (*alaṅkāra*) [merely by its own name].
For indeed, a relationship is not understood from a related term when the genitive case and so forth are omitted; nor is "flavor" (*rasa*) understood from the word "flavor" itself.
However, a designation that is not too remote [from its referent] comes into contact with the actual object.
One might ask: "Why is the cognition of similarity resorted to, rather than expressing [the meaning] directly with one's own throat? To this he says: "For the expressed meaning...
and so forth.

"As before" means that just as in previous instances such as "the tethering post," the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison was stated by way of metaphor (*rūpaka*), so too here it is stated by way of the *dīpaka* figure.
In this case, moderns consider *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) to apply because both the light and the cow are contextual (*prākaraṇika*).

However, since both are contextual, the cow possesses a superior degree of contextuality relative to the larger context, whereas the light possesses an inferior degree; with this distinction in mind, the ancients established this as *dīpaka* (illumination).
With reference to that, this particular mode of expression has been employed here.
This applies likewise to other figures of speech, such as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) and *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), and so forth;
even there, the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) need not be explicitly stated in its own words. Thus—
Wealth in times of distress, an ornament in a festival, a refuge when one's own life is in peril, and lamps in the night—
a true jewel like you is someone capable of bearing the weight of manifold requests and services.

Thus, it will be stated here that since the meaning of your statement is understood through the praise of something irrelevant (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) by virtue of its similarity [to the intended subject], it need not be stated again. We shall elaborate on this point at length in the *Bṛhatī*. In the phrase "itinaiva," the word *iti* is employed in the sense of a reason (*hetu*); when used, it functions by inherently implying that the meaning of the preceding sentence is either being asserted or made known.
The word "better" (varam) refers merely to the avoidance of the two aforementioned faults;
however, this is not entirely faultless,
because both the preceding and following words would be redundant.
Regarding "of that which is unconnected" (*anibandhanasya*): for there is no fault in [the word] by virtue of its being something to be filled and something that fills.

Regarding "without qualification" (*aviśeṣaṇa*): the meaning is that even the employment of a non-deviating [word] is praised for the purpose of providing a qualification; thus Vāmana says: "And [there is a fault] in the case of a qualifier. In the phrase "was beheld" (*vyalokyata*), the very act of beholding implies both the beholder and the world; thus, the word "world" (*loka*) is redundant.
These two [terms] are employed by virtue of their specific application and their logical necessity.
The word *gām* (accusative of *go*) need not be used because it is never excluded from the act of speaking, which is the synonym for the word *vāk*.
As for the word *dṛṣṭa*, since the very faculty of seeing (*dṛk*) is already implied as the instrument of the act of seeing, the word *dṛk* would be redundant if used again.
"In other cases of grammatical relations as well" means, for example, that in the expression "he stands in his place," there is a tautology regarding the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
However, the usage "he stands in a secluded place" is not faulty, as it is employed for the purpose of providing a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
"Only one" means that there is only one [type of] simile (*upamā*) and so forth.

"Verbal nature" (*śābdatva*) means being expressed by words such as "just like" (*yathā*); "implicit nature" (*ārthatva*) means being expressed by words such as "similar" (*sadṛśa*). "Extremely clear" means visible even to those with a coarse vision.
Regarding the phrase "Umā and the bull-bannered one":

here, although the relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison is already understood through the passage beginning with "just as by him who was born in the reeds," it is stated once again by the passage beginning with "by one similar to him.
For the poet, however, the prior relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison is intended for the purpose of [the god's] delight.
But another type [of simile] has as its cause such things as majesty (*prabhāva*) which are implied;
for instance, "This Dilīpa is a moon among kings, just as the moon [is] in the ocean of milk"—such is the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison that it establishes.

The author, however, considers that since the cognition of majesty and so forth occurs as a necessary consequence of the mention of a specific standard of comparison, there is no need to state them twice.

The meaning is as follows: when the manifestation of a certain form— such as that of a mountain and so forth— as the form of a beloved and so forth occurs through the power of the composition of words associated with specific gender markers,
then whatever simile or metaphor (*rūpaka*) is employed for that purpose, namely for the sake of perceiving that mountain as having the form of a beloved,
that is redundant.
"Uravaḥ" means large; "payodharāḥ" means clouds, and "urū ca payodharau" refers to the thighs and breasts.
"From convention" (samayāt) means they have come together.
The word "iva" (as if) is placed out of its logical order in the phrase "like a fresh nail-mark."
"Yāpitaḥ" means "passed," "spent," or "concluded.
"Only from the comparison" refers to the fresh nail-mark being given to the *palāśa* flower by virtue of its similarity in form to that mark; thus, the phrase "fresh nail-mark" is used.

"The employment of its qualifiers" means the employment of the qualifier "given during dalliance" for the fresh nail-mark, and the employment of the qualifier "by a woman whose modesty was dispelled by intoxication" for the young woman.

The word "yataḥ" (from which) means that the inference of gender—whether male or female—is derived from the indication of masculinity or femininity in the case of the fragrant forest garland (*surabhivanamālā*) and others, by means of the simile "as if a nail-mark. This is because the nature of the individual (*vyakti*) has been established as being of the form of an inference, according to the method stated in the first deliberation.
The three examples—"the bow of Indra," "excessive," and "possessing coils"—are stated in the order of their dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Because this sequence of rebirth exists,
[the roles of] protagonist and antagonist are inferred;
"is inferred" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Thus, the ellipsis is that it is inferred that "the two [peaks] are like jeweled pillars for a woman.

The serpent Vāsuki himself is the "rope" (netra) used for pulling; by means of his intense whirling, which consists of revolving in every direction, the form of Mount Mandara became agitated by its twisting and turning at the waist—that is, at its middle portion.
Likewise, the turning of the eye— the gaze— that is expansive and wide-reaching, is itself the *vibhrama* (bewildering charm) or *vilāsa* (graceful play).
By means of her form (*mūrti*), which is superimposed with the behavior of a heroine (*nāyikā*),
the surges (*utkalikā*)— both the waves and the yearnings— arise in the heart, that is, in the central region and the mind.
The phrase "for the purpose of ascending" (*ārohārtha*) is derived from the portion of the preceding verse meaning "in order to ascend" (*āroḍhum*);
and the phrase "the purpose of the heart" (*hṛdayārtha*) refers to its location in the line "the heart of the ocean" (*hṛdayam ambunidheḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "of those two": *āroha* is a specific function of the living soul (*jīva*), and *hṛdaya* is a specific part of the body of the living soul.
The status of being a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) occurs through such modes as metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on similarity, or "crooked speech" (*vakrokti*).

He says "yadartha" [in the verse] because, when words such as "heart" (hṛdaya) are used in their technical sense (lākṣaṇika), another meaning is understood even without the use of the word for the object itself (svaśabda).
Where— in the case of the subject of comparison (upameya) such as the ocean—

there is a quality (dharma) such as the heart, which is the locus of the primary purpose (yadartha) and is the object of the standard of comparison (upamāna) in the form of a hero (nāyaka) and so forth, that [quality] would be superimposed (āropita) through indication (lakṣaṇā).

The meaning is that the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between those two—the hero and others as the *upamāna*, and the ocean and others as the *upameya*—is not intended to be expressed by words (*śābda*);
rather, it is intended to be merely implied (*gamyamāna*).
In this very context, he provides an example of the fault when [the relationship] is expressed by words, beginning with the verse starting "aparāga... (free from passion).
The construction is as follows: it is easy to uproot the roots—the group of constituent elements beginning with the ministers—as well as the binding supports of a tree.
"That indeed" (*tad dhi*) expresses the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared;
"just as" (*yathā*) indicates a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
He connects [the verse] with the thought that there is either a simile (upamā) or a metaphor (rūpaka) regarding that; "passion" (anurāga) also means redness (lauhitya).
The word "also" (api) is to be construed near the words "pleasure" (sukha) and so forth.
The word *vasu* refers to both splendor (*tejas*) and wealth (*dhana*).

Here, the act of "expelling" (*niṣkāsanam*), by virtue of its intensity, establishes the courtesan's nature as a metaphor; this is the proof (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and by way of the effect," the "effect" here is the act of expelling.
"Of its particularity" means of the particularity of femininity, namely, the form of a courtesan.
"Having both meanings" refers to the employment of a word with two senses, as in "by [the woman] with pale breasts" and so forth.
"Particularity of gender" refers to cases such as "of the autumn sun" and so forth.
In such instances as "the heart to ascend to the state of virtuous conduct" (*guṇavṛtti padam āroḍhum*),
there is a specific type of simile (*upamānaviśeṣa*), as in "resembling a fresh nail-wound" (*ārdranakhakṣatābham*). Insult (*ākrośa*) refers to the giving of abusive language (*gālidāna*).

Regarding *paryāyokta* (periphrasis): by the phrase "the beauty of hardness was rendered futile in the breasts of Rāhu’s wife," the severing of Rāhu’s head is revealed through an indirect manner; thus, the meaning is that his unique instrument—the discus—is indeed perceived.

Regarding *padādi*: the sense is that alliteration (*anuprāsa*) of syllables occurring at the beginning of words and so forth, when shown through a particular mode of composition (*gumphabhaṅgī*), is exceedingly dear to poets.
Regarding the term *kalabhāṣiṇī*,
in this context the reading *kamalekṣaṇe* is appropriate for the sense;
otherwise, there would be nothing more than a mere play on sounds (*anuprāsa*).
The word *śātrava* is derived from *śatru* itself by adding the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule beginning with *prajñādi*.

As for the phrase "that very representation" (*tadrūpaṇam eva*), although a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is fit for usage because it implies a comparison (*upamā*)—since a metaphor possesses an implied similarity—it is nevertheless understood through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). Therefore, where there is an explicit mention [of the comparison], that is redundant; so what doubt could there be regarding redundancy in the case of a simile (*upamā*)?

Regarding the word *iva*: since the understanding of the meaning "as if swooning" or "causing [others] to swoon" is already established, it is well known that one who has fallen into a state of delusion due to contact with poison and the like causes others to become deluded as well. In the example "this one of dull luster," the sense "just like mine" is understood through implication (*arthāt*) and is therefore not explicitly stated.
"Mumūrcha" means "he expanded.
Regarding the phrase "the presence or absence of a sublater":

by this it is shown that where there exists a sublater of the relationship between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) for even a single qualifier, there is no fault even if they are used separately, as for example:
Only the cakorī birds are clever in the act of sipping moonlight; only the women of Avanti are skilled in the playful dalliance of love.
Regarding such cases as these, he says [it occurs] in the *prativastūpamā* (point-by-point simile).
Here, in the absence of particles such as *hi* or *iva*, there would be a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*).

Since the understanding of the contextual relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) does not result in a coherent sentence-meaning without the separate employment of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), its separate employment is not faulty.
The phrase "tadvacanam" (that statement) refers to the expression of inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) by means of the term "sahaja" (innate).
[The genitive case] in "tulyavibhaktīnām" refers to the objects of comparison (*upamāna*) and the objects compared (*upameya*), which possess identical case endings;
this is a genitive used for specification (*nirdhāraṇe*).
The meaning is "of one among these.
By the term "by synonyms" (paryāyaiḥ), it is meant by terms such as "sahaja" (innate) and so forth, which are used in place of terms such as "svābhāvika" (intrinsic) and so forth.

"By resorting to other compound words" means by resorting to a *dvandva* followed by a *tatpuruṣa*, such as "Umā and Mā are Umāme; the two husbands of them," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the words *chāyā* and *nihata*," the word *chāyā* should have been placed first and the word *nihata* second; thus, the examples were stated according to the very sequence of the point being illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*).

The expression "let it be so" (*astv iti*) refers to the usage of the words *chāyā* and *nihata*. "Of both as well" means either a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by a *dvandva*, or a *dvandva* compound preceded by a *bahuvrīhi*.

And although this was stated by way of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), its conclusion should be understood as applying to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well. For the application in the case of the subject is as follows:
it is possible for the definition [of a compound] to apply to either a *tatpuruṣa* that precedes a *dvandva*, or a *tatpuruṣa* that follows a *dvandva*.
It was stated in the investigation of the non-deliberation regarding what is to be enjoined that [the compound] is "for the sake of that";
this means "by as many words as are required.
In the present context, based on the definition of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, one should understand that it is preceded by the definition of a *dvandva* compound.
Thus, regarding the statement "it does not have the characteristic of a *dvandva*," one should understand that it is preceded by the characteristic of a *tatpuruṣa*.

"Of that" refers to the *dvandva*. "Not of that class" means where there is no suspicion of a *tatpuruṣa*; for even in the case of "Pārvatī-Parameśvarau," since we observe the employment of a *karmadhāraya* in the word "Parameśvara," it is preceded by a *tatpuruṣa*.
It should be applied as follows: in the context of the discussion on tautology (*paunaruktya*), "reflection on the intermediate" means "reflection on the compound.

Here, although the word *mādhava* is etymological (*yaugika*), because it is a conventional name (*saṃjñā*) established through common usage (*rūḍhi*), in the expression "Umā and Mādhava" (*umā-mādhavau*), [the rule applies].

They say that because there is a perception of Umā and Mādhava as being touched [by each other], rather than the sense of a *dvandva-pūrva-tatpuruṣa*, the definition of a *dvandva* is not particularly convincing here.
As for the phrase "rekhā hi," *rekhā*, *maryādā*, *avadhi*, and *sīmā* are synonyms.
In that regard, the formal argument (prayoga) by way of rejecting the class of things to be abandoned is as follows: "in saṃsāra," etc.
Here, the rejection of the abandonable consists in the refutation of the possibility of saṃsāra. The acceptance of what is to be adopted is as follows: "of the creator (tvaṣṭṛ)," etc.
Here, "the expansion of prosperity" means its extension; thus, there is the grasping of that which is to be acquired.
Regarding the phrase "whose likeness is like the rising of the moon," the word *saṃnibha* has been explained as a synonym for radiance (*prabhā*).
However, according to the *Dāṇḍin* treatise, the word *saṃnibha* is a synonym for "resembling" (*sadṛśa*); as it has been stated:
The words *iva*, *vat*, *yathā*, *samāna*, *nibha*, and *saṃnibha* [are used in this sense].
Accordingly, it should be explained that "resembling the rising of the moon" (*indūdayasaṃnibha*) means "similar to the rising of the moon" (*indūdayena sadṛśa*).
By the phrase "by that very mention," the meaning is "by the mention of being attentive."

Regarding the terms "mūḍhacetana" (one with a deluded consciousness) and "mūḍhadhiya" (one with a deluded intellect): since the state of delusion, which is the meaning of the word "moha," is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), there would be tautology between the words "consciousness" (*cetana*) and "intellect" (*dhī*). If it is argued that the understanding of that [delusion] arises through its connection to that [intellect], the meaning is that the understanding of sentience (*caitanya*) arises through its connection to the sentient being.
[The term] "kṛpāmṛdu" means tender with compassion.
If compassion (*kṛpā*) is a mental factor (*caitasa-dharma*), then the term expressing consciousness (*caitanya*) was not employed [in its definition].
The same should be stated regarding "deluded" (*mūḍha*) and "one who is deluded.
Furthermore, the phrase "whose form has arisen" (*uditavapuṣi*) merely results in tautology.

Regarding the statement, "The mind is the agent; joy is the action and the instrument," here the terms "action" (*kriyā*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*) are used in a relationship of general and particular, just as in the expression "the cow is the brindled one.

However, the author’s intention is that since only the particular [term] is useful and because the general term is never deviant, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is redundant; and since the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) already denotes action, it is superfluous. Therefore, only the word "sorrow" (*śoka*) should have been employed.
The statement that pleasure consists of the nature of a specific experience is made according to the Buddhist system;
however, the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that pleasure is indeed an insentient quality of the self, to be grasped by cognition through its inherence in the same object.
In their system, the term "experience" (*anubhava*) must necessarily be included [in the definition].

"Of one" refers to the ocean; "and of the other" refers to that which is for the purpose of crossing over. The phrase "due to the comprehension of their respective natures" is to be supplied in both cases.
Regarding the phrase "madirādrava":
here, *samābhāti* is counted as a single word because prefixes, being dependent on what they illuminate (*dyotya*), lack the status of being separate words.
The phrase "when there is the employment of one or more" means that when the employment of even one [prefix] is admitted, the others likewise possess that same status.
In that case as well, oneness is indeterminate;
in this way, the application should be made for two, three, and so forth,
because there is a multiplicity of modes due to that indeterminacy.
Regarding the phrase "caused by lack of discrimination":
although it is indeed the act of acting without reflection that constitutes the cause of misfortune,

nevertheless, because lack of discrimination is the motivator for acting without reflection, even though the former is the cause, it is the act of acting without reflection itself that is stated to be the cause.

"No," [it is argued], because when there exists a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) such as "where there is fire, there is smoke," which occurs at the time of the connection, the understanding of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, "when fire is absent, smoke is not"—which belongs to that very qualifier, is logically possible only through that same positive concomitance as its cause. This is because it would follow that the established relationship between cause and effect would be reversed; for the commencement of the cognition of negative concomitance is caused by the cognition of positive concomitance, and not the reverse.
"Because of the qualification" means that they are "greedy for qualities" because [the quality] is common [to others]. Regarding "by implication":
tautology is of two kinds—pertaining to meaning and pertaining to words.

In that context, since the meaning is established through its own capacity (*sāmarthya*), the figurative (*gauṇa*) aspect resides in the meaning because it does not appear as a tautology at first sight; the primary (*mukhya*) aspect resides in the word because it appears immediately. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the base and the suffix," it should be applied both distributively and collectively: as the meaning of the base, the meaning of the suffix, and the meaning of the combination of base and suffix.
The same should be stated regarding both the *prakṛti* (base) and the *pratyaya* (suffix);
otherwise, there would be an omission of the fivefold repetition previously specified.
[This applies to] that which has been prescribed.

When there is a suspicion that a *bahuvrīhi* compound which exists according to its actual nature might be a *karmadhāraya*, a word such as a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is employed—as in "those possessing provisions consisting of the cutting of lotus stalks" (*bisakisalayacchedapātheyavantaḥ*).
The redundancy in such a case is evident due to the cumbersome nature of employing two distinct grammatical operations (*vṛtti*).
In the example "in which [there are] *jāmbava* sprouts," etc., the meaning of "in which" refers to the word "sprout" (*pallava*).

The meaning (*artha*) here is characterized by the suffix *tya*; it is that meaning for which there is the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), namely the production of the suffix *aṇ* from that *taddhita*, resulting in its becoming an object of cognition. That which ends in such a *taddhita* suffix—such as the word *jāmbava*—is not to be compounded with the word *pallava*.
Because the meaning "jambū leaves" is already conveyed by the compound (*samāsa*), it would follow that the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is redundant.
"By the power of the qualifier" means by the greatness of qualifiers such as "Pināka-wielder" (*pinākapāṇi*).
Where one intends [to refer to] a distinguished being, such as Śiva and others, who possesses excellence and deficiency and is endowed with consciousness (*saṃjñin*), there is no tautology;
otherwise, however, there is tautology,
as for example in "May that Bhava, adorned with the cool-rayed moon, protect you."
The word *iva* and so forth expresses similarity as "just once" (*sakṛd eva*),
as in the passage beginning with "having emerged through knowledge" (*niryāya vidyā*).
The phrase "as if" (*yadvat*) summarizes by way of an illustration the passage beginning with "by people whose stumbling is unborn" (*ajātaskhalanaiḥ*).
"In the case of the meaning" refers to instances such as *rāhu-strī-ratana-yoḥ* (of Rāhu, the woman, and the jewel).
"By virtue of which" refers to instances such as *taj-jigīṣur iva* (as if desiring to conquer that).
Alternatively, it refers to cases where the cognition of an action arises by virtue of a specific *kāraka*, or the cognition of a *kāraka* arises by virtue of a specific action.
In this context, the meaning is that the employment of both the action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kāraka*) should not be used,
as in the example "mā bhavantam" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "yo yaddharma" (that which has such-and-such a property), in the example "aparadiggaṇikā" (the courtesan of the western direction) and so forth, the object characterized by the direction— which is marked metaphorically by the properties of the courtesan, such as being driven out— is what is intended.

Likewise, in such instances as "He churned the ocean," the meaning characterized by the ocean— which is not syntactically connected [to the literal sense] because it belongs to a lover (kāmuka) whose heart and so forth are being churned— is not accepted as a verbal metaphor (śābdī rūpaka), since it consists of the metaphorical representation of the ocean as a courtesan and her lover.
The *ārthī* [vṛtti], however, is indeed accepted;
it occurs only within those [words] that are employed [as compounds], as in the case of *madirādrava* and so forth.
Regarding the rule "when the agent (*kartṛ*) [is expressed]," it refers to the agent such as the king who is the primary [referent].

And when the action of that [cutting]— namely, the act of cutting with a sword— is established as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), the verbal expression of its many subordinate parts, such as the falling of the blade’s edge and so forth, is not accepted,
just as in the case of the phrase "held in the hand" (*karakalita*) and similar examples.
This is what is meant.

In the case of a king or similar agent performing an action such as cutting, even the mention of the sword or other instruments—which are the most effective means (*sādhakatama*)—is not desired for their own constituent parts, such as the edge or the striking motion; this is because those intermediate parts are already implied by that very instrument which serves as the primary factor.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that two faults would apply [if one were to specify them], namely the faults of *prayukta* (redundancy) and *kartari* (specifying the agent).
The word "te" (those) refers to compounds.

Regarding the phrase "in a [grammatical] formation" (*vṛttau*): whether in a compound or a sentence, where there is a non-common qualifier (*asādhāraṇa-viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) need not be explicitly expressed, as in the case of *duḥkhānubhava* and so forth.

The meaning is that since there is no deviation from the nature of water and so forth in the case of tears and the like—expressed as "whatever is of such a nature"—one should not employ words such as "water" when there is no purpose for doing so, as in the expression "tears of water in the eyes.

Similarly, regarding the phrase "whatever belongs to whatever": if a property such as trickling is an invariable attribute of a subject such as a moonstone, the composition of those two [words] is not recommended.
As in the example beginning with "the eyes of the wives of his enemies" and so forth; "otherwise" means for the purpose of similarity (sādharmya).

Regarding the term "action" (*kriyā*): the cognition of an action characterized by grief and so forth does not deviate from the cognition of its instrument (*karaṇa*), because action is nothing other than the instrument itself.

In the absence of the cognition of that [instrument], and thus the absence of the cognition of the instrument, that very action characterized by grief and so forth would not be ascertained, due to their identity.
In the expression "the act of relinquishing" (*tyāga-kriyā*), this alone is the ground for the application of the word "action."
Therefore,

for that reason— namely, by virtue of the employment of words such as "sorrow" (*śoka*) and so forth, whatever instrument (*karaṇa*) is manifested or made manifest, when that [instrument] is expressed through the employment of words such as "sorrow," one should not employ a word for that [instrument],
just as in the case of [the expression] "of the instrument of the action of sorrow" (*śokakriyākaraṇasya*), and so on. This is the meaning.
The phrase "and when applied" (*prayukte ca*) is a summary of the four types of redundancy, beginning with redundancy of the base form (*prakṛti*).
The phrase "mutually" (*anyonya*) includes the redundancy of the sentence (*vākya*). The expression "of both" refers to any one [redundancy] occurring from within either of the two.
It does not escape redundancy,
as in the case of "one should act impulsively" and so forth.
Having thus examined the redundancy in detail, he says, "How there is the non-utterance of that which is to be uttered," in order to elaborate upon the non-expression of the expressible.
This concise indication is intended to imply, by way of a side-glance, the expression of the inexpressible, which will be discussed later as following the same logical principle.

The reference is made by means of the word "this" (*idam*), because it serves as the cause for uncontradicted direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and thereby eliminates error; and because direct perception is worthy of being referred to by way of its object.
Regarding its expression by its own word: when a pronoun already exists, its representation once again by its own word—
that is, the further designation by its own word of an object already fit for reference by a pronoun— is the redundancy of the word.
Thus it was stated redundantly;
now, however, by means of its own term as the representative of all [other] names, the expression or non-expression of what is to be expressed is being discussed.
Regarding the phrase "the property-possessor and the property," the property-possessor (*dharmin*) is the object characterized as Hara.
Dharma is the state of being censurable due to its connection with a skull;
both [the subject and the predicate] consist of the substratum (dharmin) and its property (dharma).
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of apprehending the particular," the "particular" here refers to the state of being censurable.
The word "tasya" (of that) refers to the state of being censurable;
this should be understood as applying to the phrase "evaṃ tasya vivakṣita" (thus, his intended [meaning]).
The intended meaning is characterized by pitiable wretchedness.
The term "ārtha" [is used] by way of a qualifier because of its existence;
for example, in the expression "vāmalocanatvam.
And here, "vāmalocanā" is not the substantive (viśeṣya) word.
Furthermore, because of the force of the two sentence-meanings produced by the pair of words "yat" and "tat," there is the cognition of the substantive characterized as the heroine (*nāyikā*).
In this context, the term *vāmalocanā* (beautiful-eyed one) is merely an adjective.
The third [type] is called "residing in both."
"And not that" refers to the repetition [of the word].
"And not of these" refers to these types by means of that very same pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in its respective turn. "Because of the smallness of the fault" means...
Regarding the word "tasya" (of him), because it connects with a term separated [in the sequence], some degree of excellence must be understood;
thus, it should be stated as "by his prayer for union.
This is because there is a difference in meaning.
The meaning is this: every repetition is a multiple occurrence of a single [action], just as a bronze vessel is used repeatedly for the meals of the poor.
Thus it has been said: "Repetition is multiple occurrence."

Furthermore, it is not logical for a word to be unitary when there is a difference in meaning, because the difference in meaning— which is the primary factor— is what differentiates the word, which is subordinate to it.

Therefore, in this case, the actual similarity between two words and the delusion of unity among perceivers caused by that similarity are the basis for this very usage of the term "repetition" (*āvṛtti*) in its primary sense.
"And for this reason" means:
because repetition is not logical,
for that reason.
"Consisting of the subject, the property, and both" means that [the reason] is intended to be established in a thing that consists of both;
this is expressed by the words "wherein another," and so forth.
In the context of providing examples for what should and should not be expressed, he examines *śleṣa* (punning) at length in terms of its possessing qualities and defects.
Regarding the phrase "alakālī":
the hair-tufts themselves are the swarm of bees, and the swarm of bees is like the hair-tufts.
*Chada* means a lip or a petal;
*āmoda* means joy or fragrance;
and *karṇikā* means an ear-ornament or the seed-vessel.
"Not [the province] of *śleṣa* (punning).
But surely, in the context of *śleṣa*, what occasion is there for a discussion regarding the lotus as a point of comparison?
This is not so.

The intention is that since there is no object distinct from other figures of speech, and because *śleṣa* (paronomasia) subverts all other figures, it is only *śleṣa*—not *upamā* (simile)—that is logically appropriate here as the cause for the emergence of the semblance of a simile.
For this very reason, it was stated [in the commentary] that "but in the case of *śleṣa*, it [the simile] is merely expressed" (*vācyatayā*).
The term "composition" (*nibandha*) is used in the sense of "those who compose" (*nibadhnanti*).
"That similarity" refers to the similarity with a rope and so forth;
"not of the *śleṣa*" means not of the simile-cum-*śleṣa*.
Therefore, it should not be said that [the phrase] "like qualities" (*guṇā iva*) expresses a rope and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that *samāsokti* (condensed expression) is based on the similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*), yet [in this instance] they do not employ such qualifiers? To this he replies: "For it is not merely the similarity of qualifiers," and this has been determined by us in the *Harṣacaritavārtika*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. By the word "him" (*tam*) in the phrase "having separately taken him up" (*pṛthak tam upādāya*), the moon (*śaśin*) is referred to.

For that [comparison] exists only when there is a real object; this is the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared. Regarding the domain of *śleṣa* (punning), there are here three stages.

Because the word *rāja* has both meanings, there is a paronomasia (*śleṣa*). Without resorting to that, there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) by means of [the moon] being identified with the moon; and following upon that, there is a simile (*upamā*) in the form "like the moon. Now, one might object: in the case of *rājendu*, since there is no evidence for or against accepting either the simile or the metaphor, a commixture (*saṅkara*) is more appropriate.
Metaphor (*rūpaka*) is not necessarily [present];
so how is it said that "metaphor is indicated" (*āsūtrita*)?
It is replied:
The metaphor (*rūpaka*) was adopted out of fear of tautology, because the intention was to proceed toward a simile (*upamā*).
However, in the absence of that simile, a commixture (*saṅkara*) would have been more appropriate here.
Alternatively, the metaphor was resorted to because it is perceived more clearly than the simile within this compound.
Indeed, with this very intention he will say: "In the domain of metaphor (rūpaka), [the rule] is as in the case of simile (upamā)";
that is, "to compete with those two," meaning with the two types of metaphor, namely, the pun-based metaphor (śleṣarūpaka) and the [other].
"Of those two, as before" means that,
in comparison with simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka) [is more common], and in comparison with metaphor, paronomasia (śleṣa) [is more common].
"Now, if this were so" introduces an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this fault: that even sunlight (*ātapa*) would be heat (*tāpa*).
The fruit includes rice and so forth;
*sumanas* refers even to flowers;
and *khalatā* is the state of being wicked.
And it is the place for grinding grain and so forth;
being non-existent, it is to be defiled and is unseemly—
this is what is meant by "ornament."

In examples such as *khalatām*, where a pun (*śleṣa*) is evoked by a simile (*upamā*), the simile does not sublate the pun; for the latter lacks a distinct domain of its own. However, it is logical that the pun should sublate the simile.

Since this principle applies to other figures of speech as well, it is stated that "whatever is called an *alaṅkāra* [is so] because it contains pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding the phrase "in the absence of another basis": if there were a basis such as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), then—as in the previous case—the simile suggested by *śleṣa* (punning) would not need to be employed.
Nor should it be argued that this is a case of *samāsokti* (condensed expression) due to the similarity of qualifiers such as "not rejected" (*anirākṛta*) and so forth;

for there is no perception of these qualifiers being restricted to the object of comparison alone. Here, the term "suspicion regarding the subject" (*viṣayatāśaṅkā*) means the possibility of its being the subject of a simile (*upamā*).
In some places, however, the reading is *tadatadviṣayatā*.

In that case, the meaning is that one should not simultaneously suspect both the status of being the object of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and the status of being the object of *upamā* (simile), because these two are established as having the relationship of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*).
[The phrase] "due to the two aforementioned defects" refers to this.

It has been stated that there are two defects regarding the subject of *śleṣa* (paronomasia)—namely, where *śleṣa* is employed in the domain of *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), and where *upamā* (simile) is employed in the domain of *śleṣa*.
The meaning is that, in this case, there is no connection between them.
As for the phrase "that which is an ornament" (*yadalaṅkāra*).
For the purpose of manifesting figures of speech such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *upamā* (simile), there are words such as "like a lotus" (*abjam iva*) and so forth;

if another figure, such as *samāsokti* (condensed expression) or *śleṣa*, were to be manifested by those very same words— though perhaps in fewer instances and without [explicit] terms like "like a lotus"—
then that *samāsokti*, *śleṣa*, or other figure should be accepted because of its brevity.
The meaning is that there is no other [figure], such as *śleṣopamā* (pun-based simile) and so forth.
Now, one might object: "The defining characteristic of other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is that they serve as causes for an excellence of beauty; that [characteristic] is now being specified."
To the question, "How then was this stated? he replies: "For there is not [such a thing as] 'it does not exist'.
In producing their own excellence of beauty (*śobhātiśaya*), there is no distinction among the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*);
therefore, it is not logical to say that one is accepted while another is rejected.
The intended meaning is that this [distinction] is appropriate only by relying on relative weight (gurulaghutva) and not otherwise.

This was stated with reference to the excellence of the expressed (vācya); however, the specific difference with reference to the suggested (pratīyamāna) will be explained immediately hereafter. Furthermore, by the words "And what more... and so forth, he states that the cause for the accomplishment of beauty in the composition of poetry is the accomplishment of ornaments (alaṅkāra), which follows as a secondary result, just as in the case of a speaker regarding pain and disease.
"Only by means of the figures of speech *samāsokti* (synecdoche) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
By *samāsokti*, as in the example "alakālī" (*alaka-ālī*), etc.; by *śleṣa*, as in the example "Bhairavācārya," etc.
Regarding "nopamāyā":
in examples such as *alakālī*, there is a simile based on paronomasia (*śleṣopamā*);
in examples such as *bhairavācārya*, the simile itself constitutes the simile (*upamaivopamā*).

In this context, according to the sequence of this very text, the passage beginning with "as in the case of simile" (*yathopamāyā*) appears to have been interpolated into the section concerning metaphor (*rūpaka*),
because metaphor is not concluded here,

and because the two aforementioned defects are not established [for it]. Furthermore, since this previous passage is deficient in this respect, it is for this reason that it is not read in some manuscripts.
If, however, there were no insertion [of the word "rūpaka"], one would have to include the phrase "possessing the three forms" here.
Therefore, either that textual passage must be excluded, or the term "rūpaka" must be inserted here.
Furthermore, the phrase "due to the two aforementioned faults" has been explained according to the propriety of the context.
"For by its accomplishment" means that when the accomplishment of rasa and *bandha* occurs, the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) necessarily follow.
Here, "productive capacity" (*niṣpādakatva*) refers to the capacity for measurement (*māpakatva*).
For this very reason, regarding Bharata’s statement that "the production of rasa [occurs]," it should be explained as "the inference of rasa.
Its "variety" refers to the variety of the determinants (vibhāvas) and so forth.
The meaning is that these, being the basis of that [variety], are ultimately the causes for the cognition of rasa by being the basis of rasa through a traditional sequence.
Regarding the phrase "therefore, for these":

the poet must primarily achieve beauty residing in the meaning (artha), not the formal employment of figures of speech (alaṅkāra), because figures of speech are subordinate as they are invariably concomitant with that [beauty of meaning].
Therefore, their composition should be carried out in such a way that beauty is produced;
the meaning is that the introduction, removal, and so forth of these figures are for that very purpose.
By stating that there is no "daily" (or routine) introduction or removal and so on, the specific distinction of how the figures mutually produce beauty is established.
Furthermore, the absence of any distinction was previously stated in the passage beginning with "for there is no [difference] in its own nature" and so forth;
how then is there no contradiction?
This is not so.
Previously, the absence of any distinction was established with the intention of focusing on the production of beauty through the process of instruction (*avavadhāna*).

Here, however, a distinction is stated in terms of the relative weight and so forth of the *vibhāvas* and other poetic factors as instruments; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever due to this difference in perspective.
The phrase "by some" refers to Vāmana and others.

Now, that which was established by mere assertion—that because a word lacks any other power, its function as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) is impossible—is set forth in a concise rule (*sūtra*) to be demonstrated in connection with the topic of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), for the purpose of providing examples where what is denoted is not expressed: "And this [is]...
The meaning is: that which was treated in the context of *samāsokti* (condensed expression) and that in whose context *upamā* (simile) was treated.

The term "twofold" implies that the *ubhayaśleṣa* (double pun), which will be discussed later, is included right here, because it arises from the combination of these two very [types of *śleṣa*]. Regarding the phrase "where there is no deficiency": where the qualification of the substantive neither falls short nor exceeds [its referent].
In this context, there is a *śleṣa* (punning connection).
The inclusion of the word "mātra" (only) is for the purpose of embracing those words capable of being connected to both [the agent and the object], despite the difference in gender and number.
[The term] "kartṛkarma" (agent and object) [is used].

The meaning is that where the primary sense—whether in the form of an agent, an object, or, by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," an action—is led to lose its own nature through *śleṣa* (punning), there *śleṣa* is not faultless.
Furthermore, that [faultless *śleṣa*] is twofold: having as its object words that express a property (*dharma*) and having as its object words that express a substratum (*dharmin*).
However, the status of being the object of words that express both [meanings] will be refuted later.
"But the other," however, refers to semantic punning (*arthaśleṣa*).

In both cases—whether it be a *śabdaśleṣa* (phonetic pun) or an *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun)—as long as a basis such as "as if" (*iva*) is not employed, the second meaning remains entirely without authority; therefore, a basis must be resorted to for the manifestation of the *śleṣa*. Regarding the phrase "in this interval": [it refers to Śiva] whose white laughter is like that of one possessing a blossoming smile, [a smile] consisting of those market-stalls or the great ramparts of the triple and quadruple cities of Tripura which are white with full-blown jasmine flowers.

Concluding the pair of seasons consisting of the spring (the season of flowers) and the two months that resemble it in beauty, as well as the Kṛta age and the others, Mahākāla— the long duration of time, and also a specific deity who is the agent of destruction— opened his mouth and became manifest;
this is an example of *samāsokti* (synecdoche).

In the expression "Mahākāla," when the unconnected qualifying term "mahāsamaya" (the Great Pledge) is employed as the substantive, the specific deity is understood solely through the similarity of the qualifiers; thus, *samāsokti* (synecdoche) occurs, serving as the proof for the non-repetition (*anāvṛtti*) of the word "Mahākāla. Furthermore, there is no effort whatsoever required here in the employment of the word "Mahākāla."
Lest it be suspected that the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is redundant due to the *samāsokti* (synecdoche), as in the case of "Alakā and the Kali age," [the author says] "covered":
in the sense of the mountain, that by which the directions and the sky— the atmosphere— were covered because of its vastness.
Let it be proclaimed loudly: [the mountain] which stands treading upon the earth and the sky,
whose horns and peaks possess great height and circumference, and by virtue of its fitness, bears the crescent moon shimmering upon its head.
The meaning is: who would not be struck with wonder upon seeing such a lord of the mountain, the king of mountains?
In the case of [the deity] Hara, however, he is one by whom the very quarters of space have been made his lower garment and thus covered;
likewise, he stands mounted upon a bull with thick horns.

The meaning is: who would not be filled with wonder upon directly perceiving the Lord of Mountains, Kailāsa’s sovereign, endowed with the crescent moon upon his head, and feeling himself graced by that very sight?

The phrase "like 'the white horse runs'" (*śveto dhāvati*) refers to the primacy of the word (*śabdatantra*), whereas "like a lamp" (*pradīpavat*) refers to the primacy of the meaning (*arthatantra*).
